The findings suggest that college students' sleep problems may be embedded within a broader system of health behaviors and psychological processes. Given the cross-sectional design, future longitudinal or experimental studies should examine the dynamic associations among these variables.

papers.title: Food craving in a cultural context: behavioral and electrophysiological evidence from Indian and Western food sets.
papers.abstract: Food craving is a ubiquitous experience, often shaped by cultural familiarity. Although craving may be considered a culture-bound construct, its neural and behavioral underpinnings across food cultures remain limited. Here, we examined the effects of multisensory food exposure on craving in an Indian population, comparing Indian and Western foods across sweet and savory categories. In Experiment 1 (Indian Food Craving; IFC), participants viewed Indian sweet and savory food images before and after multisensory exposure, reporting desire and willingness-to-pay (bid) ratings along with Food Craving Questionnaire-State (FCQ-S) scores. EEG was recorded using a 64-channel system. In Experiment 2 (Western Food Craving; WFC), participants completed a similar paradigm using Western food items. Multisensory exposure significantly increased FCQ-S scores in both experiments, indicating successful craving induction. Behaviorally, desire and bid ratings increased for both sweet and savory Indian foods, whereas for Western foods, increases were observed only for sweet items. ERP analyses revealed increased P200 and N200 amplitudes following exposure to Indian sweet foods, while LPP amplitudes increased for savory foods across both Indian and Western food categories. Complementary MVPA revealed enhanced pre- vs. post-exposure classification for sweet foods during the early (0-300 ms) window for both Indian and Western foods, whereas both sweet and savory foods showed significant classification during the later(300-600 ms) window. Together, these findings suggest that multisensory exposure modulates food-cue processing in a stimulus- and time-dependent manner, with possible contributions from attentional processes. Overall, the findings highlight the influence of food type and cultural context on craving-related neural and behavioral responses.

papers.title: Effects of acceptance and commitment therapy on psychological and health-related outcomes in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is frequently accompanied by psychological and functional impairments. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a third-wave behavioral intervention focusing on psychological flexibility, has been increasingly applied in stroke rehabilitation. Although previous reviews have suggested beneficial effects of ACT in stroke patients, whether these benefits persist in the short term after the intervention ends, and the certainty of the evidence, remain unclear. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108). Randomized controlled trials evaluating ACT in stroke patients were included. Pooled effects were calculated using random-effects models, with separate analyses for post-intervention and follow-up outcomes. Sources of heterogeneity were explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Twenty-two RCTs involving 1,975 participants were included. ACT may be associated with reductions in depressive symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.32, 95% CI: -1.80 to -0.84; follow-up: SMD = -0.76, 95% CI: -1.07 to -0.45) and anxiety symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.36, 95% CI: -1.90 to -0.82; follow-up: SMD = -0.51, 95% CI: -1.42 to 0.40, not significant); depressive symptoms remained statistically significant at follow-up. Heterogeneity was considerable for both outcomes at post-intervention (I2 = 93.68% for depression and 93.60% for anxiety), so the pooled estimates represent average effects across studies. ACT may also be associated with improvements in psychological flexibility, quality of life, and sleep quality; however, these outcomes were based on a limited number of studies and showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 74.68 to 92.26%), so they should be interpreted cautiously. However, no statistically significant effects were observed for activities of daily living, neurological function, or hope. ACT did not appear to increase dropout rates in the available studies (K = 16; RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.58-1.69). Meta-regression analyses indicated that intervention duration may not be a significant moderator of treatment effects. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, mainly due to risk of bias and inconsistency. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy may be a useful adjunctive intervention for improving psychological outcomes in people with stroke. However, evidence for functional recovery remains insufficient. Future high-quality RCTs with standardized protocols, larger samples, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm the long-term effectiveness of ACT. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifer CRD420261325108.

papers.title: Decomposition of gender disparities in abnormal sleep duration among Chinese older adults: evidence from a national survey.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is an important component of healthy aging, yet gender differences in short and long sleep among older adults remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to examine gender differences in sleep duration among Chinese older adults and quantify the contributions of socioeconomic, behavioral, functional, and health-related factors to these differences. Data were obtained from 9,590 adults aged ≥65 years who participated in the 2018 wave of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey. Sleep duration was self-reported and categorized as short (<6 h), normal (6-8 h), or long (>8 h). Multinomial logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with short and long sleep, with weighted analyses and Poisson regression performed as sensitivity analyses. Separate Fairlie decomposition analyses were conducted for short and long sleep to quantify the contributions of observed characteristics to gender differences. Overall, 44.95% of participants had abnormal sleep duration, with a higher prevalence among women than men (46.87% vs. 42.66%, p < 0.001). Compared with men, women had a higher relative risk of short sleep (RRR = 1.399, 95% CI: 1.204-1.625) but a lower relative risk of long sleep (RRR = 0.856, 95% CI: 0.754-0.972). The association with short sleep remained significant in the weighted analysis (RRR = 1.530, 95% CI: 1.210-1.935), whereas the gender difference in long sleep was attenuated (RRR = 0.821, 95% CI: 0.661-1.021). For short sleep, observed characteristics explained 21.65% of the gender disparity. Education (22.75%), depressive symptoms (11.07%), IADL limitation (6.02%), and self-assessed health (4.82%) contributed positively to the disparity, whereas smoking status (-22.57%), drinking status (-12.45%), and exercise (-4.87%) partially offset it. The gender difference in long sleep was negligible, with substantial offsetting contributions across factors. Gender differences in sleep duration among Chinese older adults were primarily concentrated in short sleep, with women experiencing a higher risk. Socioeconomic, behavioral, psychological, and functional characteristics contributed to this disparity, although most of the short-sleep difference remained unexplained. Gender-sensitive interventions addressing educational disadvantage, depressive symptoms, functional limitations, and health behaviors may help reduce inequalities in sleep duration among older adults.

papers.title: Incremental predictive value of multimodal over unimodal assessment for upper limb motor recovery after stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Clinical scales predict post-stroke motor recovery but are insensitive to neural substrates. Neuroimaging and neurophysiological biomarkers capture corticospinal integrity, yet their incremental value over clinical assessment remains unquantified. To quantify the pooled incremental predictive value (ΔAUC) of adding biomarkers to clinical models for upper limb motor recovery at 3-6 months post-stroke. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science from inception to January 31, 2026, for prospective cohort studies evaluating ≥2 assessment modalities. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled ΔAUC between multimodal and clinical-only models. Sensitivity analyses used alternative between-study variance estimators and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Meta-regression examined sources of heterogeneity. Risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS. Twenty-three studies (N = 1,341) were included. Multimodal assessment significantly improved prognostic accuracy over clinical models alone (pooled ΔAUC = +0.112, 95% CI 0.061 to 0.163, p < 0.001). MEP status showed the largest incremental gain (ΔAUC = +0.150, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.277; I 2 = 71.0%). Ipsilesional CST FA was reported in one study (ΔAUC = +0.220, 95% CI 0.110 to 0.330). Other DTI-derived metrics did not reach statistical significance (ΔAUC = +0.074, 95% CI -0.006 to 0.155). Task-based fMRI showed promise in one study (ΔAUC = +0.190, 95% CI 0.088 to 0.292). EEG, kinematic parameters, and resting-state fMRI could not be pooled. Stroke phase was a significant moderator (β = -0.127, 95% CI -0.247 to -0.007, p = 0.039), with larger gains in subacute versus acute assessments. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, adding selected biomarkers to clinical assessment was associated with improved discrimination for upper limb motor recovery after stroke. MEP status showed the largest incremental gain. Stroke phase significantly moderated the incremental value, with larger gains in the subacute phase. However, given the small number of studies and the prediction interval crossing zero, these findings should be considered statistically promising but not yet robust enough to guide routine clinical practice. Further validation in larger prospective cohorts is needed before MEP-guided stratification can be applied clinically. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261288506, Identifier: CRD420261288506.

papers.title: Source-resolved electroencephalogram microstates reveal opposing prefrontal-posterior dynamics and a candidate temporal-to-precuneus pathway in disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: Objective and circuit-level biomarkers of consciousness are urgently needed for disorders of consciousness. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from 33 patients with disorders of consciousness (17 vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, 16 minimally conscious state) and 19 healthy controls during rest and auditory stimulation, and combined source-localized microstate analysis with hypothesis-generating Granger causality analysis. Source microstate 3 (right prefrontal) and microstate 4 (parieto-occipital-temporal) showed diametrically opposite dynamics: microstate 3 was enhanced in the vegetative state whereas microstate 4 coverage and occurrence were higher in the minimally conscious state, revealing a fronto-posterior opponent imbalance. In repeated internal cross-validation within this cohort, microstate 4 occurrence discriminated the two patient groups (area under the curve = 0.812, 95% confidence interval 0.647-0.945). Hypothesis-generating connectivity analysis nominally implicated stronger right middle temporal-to-precuneus information flow in the minimally conscious state, a signal that did not survive network-level multiplicity correction. Source-resolved microstates thus reveal opposing cortical dynamics associated with consciousness level.

papers.title: Sleep duration and systemic inflammation assessed using the systemic inflammation response index: The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2017-2020 and 2021-2023.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo examine the association between usual weekday/workday sleep duration and the systemic inflammation response index among adults reporting at least 7 h of sleep while assessing the influence of questionnaire coding and complex survey design.MethodsThis cross-sectional secondary analysis included 10,971 participants aged ≥18 years from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey January 2017 to March 2020 and August 2021 to August 2023 cycles. The systemic inflammation response index was calculated as monocyte count × neutrophil count/lymphocyte count. Unweighted pooled linear models were retained as exploratory analyses after correcting smoking skip-pattern and special-response coding; the fully adjusted sample comprised 9051 participants. Survey-weighted regressions were fitted separately by period using the appropriate examination or phlebotomy weight, strata, and primary sampling units. An existing smooth curve was retained for descriptive purposes, not threshold inference.ResultsIn the corrected pooled fully adjusted model, each additional reported hour was associated with a 0.0371 higher systemic inflammation response index (95% confidence interval: 0.0198-0.0544; p < 0.001). The corresponding period-specific survey-weighted estimates were 0.0246 (95% confidence interval: -0.0108, 0.0601; p = 0.165) before the pandemic and 0.0529 (95% confidence interval: 0.0126-0.0933; p = 0.014) in 2021-2023. Fully adjusted log-Systemic inflammation response index analyses did not reach statistical significance (p < 0.05) in either period. The visual downturn near 11 h was not a formally estimated threshold; only 195 participants reported ≥12 h of sleep.ConclusionsLonger reported sleep within the ≥7 h range was positively associated with the systemic inflammation response index in exploratory pooled analyses; however, period-specific and outcome-scale checks did not provide uniformly significant evidence. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish causality, an optimal sleep duration, or an anti-inflammatory benefit of prolonged sleep duration.
papers.journal: The Journal of international medical research

papers.title: How to use Quality Improvement to enhance the portfolio for promotion and tenure in Academic Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine.
papers.abstract: Quality Improvement (QI) is a cornerstone for improving patient care and health care systems. However, QI activities are not always recognized within traditional promotion and tenure (P&T) pathways. As a result, faculty with significant QI expertise and impactful contributions may lack clear mechanisms and pathways for academic recognition, promotion, and career advancement. Identifying a clear QI P&T pathway may incentivize faculty to pursue QI as a career. Standardized approaches that translate QI activities into key conventional academic metrics and are documented across multiple domains for P&T are needed to address these gaps. The purpose of this manuscript is to provide a framework for Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine faculty to align QI work with traditional promotion criteria and encourage institutions to recognize the value and scope of QI in P&T considerations. This framework highlights strategies for documenting QI contributions across academic areas such as clinical care, education, research and service and supports faculty considering the value of pursuing an academic career in QI in Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep medicine.
keywords: ATS QIIC=ATS Quality Improvement and Implementation Committee

papers.title: Chronobiology of Aging: Interactions Between Circadian Rhythms, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation.
papers.abstract: Chronodisruption is increasingly recognised as a fundamental driver of biological aging rather than merely a consequence of advancing age. Although substantial evidence links circadian dysfunction with individual age-related diseases, the mechanistic integration of chronodisruption across the hallmarks of aging and its therapeutic implications remains fragmented. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence describing how age-associated deterioration of the circadian timing system interacts with established hallmarks of aging, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated nutrient sensing, impaired proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence. This article also incorporates how these interconnected mechanisms contribute to the development and progression of major age-related disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic diseases, and cancer, highlighting shared molecular regulators such as BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, REV-ERBs, SIRT1, AMPK, and mTOR. Although several reviews exist that focus on individual diseases or isolated circadian mechanisms, this review integrates molecular, cellular, and translational evidence into a unified framework linking chronodisruption to systemic aging. This article discusses emerging chronotherapeutic strategies including chrono-phototherapy, chrono-nutrition, chrono-exercise, natural chrono-modulators, chrono-pharmacology, and precision geromedicine that aim to restore circadian homeostasis and improve healthy aging. Collectively, this review identifies circadian rhythm restoration as a promising systems-level therapeutic approach and outlines future directions for integrating chronobiology into precision interventions for age-related diseases.
papers.journal: The journals of gerontology. Series A, Biological sciences and medical sciences

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction in Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Emerging Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, with hallmark pathological features including amyloid-beta plaques, tau tangles, and neuronal loss. The glymphatic system, a recently discovered network responsible for brain waste clearance, plays a crucial role in maintaining cerebral homeostasis by facilitating the removal of neurotoxic metabolites, including amyloid-beta. Disruption of glymphatic function has emerged as a key factor in AD pathophysiology, contributing to the accumulation of toxic proteins and accelerating neurodegenerative processes. This narrative review explores the complex interplay between glymphatic dysfunction and AD. We discuss the mechanisms of the glymphatic system, emphasizing its reliance on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid flow to clear metabolic waste, and how this process is closely linked to sleep cycles. In AD, impaired glymphatic function, exacerbated by aging and sleep disturbances, accelerates the buildup of amyloid-beta and tau, driving neurodegeneration. Furthermore, sleep disturbances commonly observed in AD patients further hinder glymphatic activity, creating a vicious cycle that exacerbates cognitive decline. Emerging therapeutic approaches aimed at enhancing glymphatic function-including sleep regulation, pharmacological agents, and lifestyle interventions-are promising, but most findings remain preliminary and largely based on animal studies or early clinical observations. These strategies should therefore be considered exploratory until validated in large-scale human trials. By restoring efficient waste clearance, such interventions may offer novel avenues for slowing or preventing AD progression.

papers.title: Integrative therapies for symptom management in dementia from a palliative perspective: narrative review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Dementia affects over 55 million people worldwide, with behavioral and psychological symptoms (BPSD) impacting over 90% of individuals. Conventional pharmacotherapies offer limited benefits with substantial side effects. Integrative care therapies (ICT) represent a complementary approach, yet the evidence supporting their use has been largely absent from the palliative care literature. This narrative review synthesizes ICT systematic reviews and meta-analyses to bridge this gap. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2015 and June 2026 evaluating ICT for dementia symptom management. Seminal earlier works were also included when updated reviews were unavailable. Individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs), validation studies, and non-English publications were excluded, except selected sources cited for mechanistic, safety, regulatory, or pivotal-trial context. Cognitive stimulation achieved the highest evidence certainty, with high-certainty evidence for communication and social interaction and moderate-certainty evidence for cognition, quality of life (QOL), and challenging behaviors. Music therapy showed moderate-certainty evidence for depression improvement but not agitation. Light therapy and movement-based mind-body therapies (MBT) demonstrated benefit across the broadest range of domains-including cognition, BPSD, and sleep-though certainty remained low-to-very-low. Massage and aromatherapy showed consistent short-term benefits for agitation and depression. Acupuncture augmented conventional medication for improvement in cognition and activities of daily living (ADL). Dietary and herbal therapies contributed primarily to cognitive domains, with Ginkgo biloba showing the most robust BPSD evidence. Cannabinoids showed preliminary evidence for agitation and in severe disease. Across modalities, effects were often limited to the treatment period, early-stage disease showed the most robust benefits, and safety profiles were favorable. Only cognitive stimulation and music therapy achieved moderate or higher Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) ratings. Multiple ICT modalities show promising evidence for dementia symptom management that aligns with palliative care principles, though most evidence is of low-to-very-low certainty. Future research should prioritize pragmatic trials in hospice and palliative care settings using outcomes meaningful to this context, including comfort, caregiver experience, and healthcare utilization.

papers.title: Prevalence, Incidence, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome in Primary Care in the United Kingdom Between 1998 and 2025.
papers.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a multisystemic disorder with a wide range of health consequences. We sought to describe temporal trends in the prevalence and incidence of PMOS and to characterize its clinical presentation, comorbidity burden, and pharmacological management in primary care in the United Kingdom (UK) between 1998 and 2025. Population-based matched cohort study using primary care records from the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink. Females newly diagnosed with PMOS between the ages of 15 and 49 matched on age, general practice, calendar year of cohort entry, and duration of medical history to population controls without PMOS. Annual prevalence and incidence of diagnosed PMOS; baseline prevalence and incidence of cardinal PMOS features and various comorbidities; and pre- and post-cohort entry prevalence of hormonal contraceptive, anti-androgen, ovulation-inducing drug, and metformin use. The prevalence of diagnosed PMOS increased from < 0.1% in 1998 to 2.0% in 2025, with incidence rising from 0.1 to 3.6 per 1,000 person-years over the same period. Among 125,482 patients with newly diagnosed PMOS matched with an equal number of controls, patients with PMOS had higher baseline prevalence and incidence of cardinal features of PMOS, as well as diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, sleep apnea, thyroid disorders, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. Use of anti-androgens, ovulation-inducing drugs, and metformin was substantially higher in patients with PMOS, especially in the year following diagnosis. PMOS is increasingly diagnosed in UK primary care and is associated with substantial multimorbidity and pharmacotherapy.

papers.title: Maternal exposure to sleep aids and risk of specific birth defects in the Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms are often reported during pregnancy, prompting use of pharmacologic treatments. We explored associations between treatments used during the month before through the third month of pregnancy ("early pregnancy") and risk of birth defects using Birth Defects Study to Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS (BD-STEPS) data from 2014-2021. Pregnancies affected by birth defects ("cases") were identified from surveillance systems in seven states; liveborn infants without birth defects ("controls") were randomly selected from the same catchment areas. Mothers of cases and controls reported early pregnancy exposures via interview, including use of prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal sleep aids. For defects with ≥5 exposed cases, we used Firth's logistic regression to estimate propensity score-adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, previous live birth, history of depression/anxiety, early pregnancy use of antipsychotics, anxiolytics, antidepressants, opioids, cigarettes, alcohol, and prenatal vitamins, occurrence of stressful events, occupation outside the home, health insurance, and site. Overall, 237 (7%) cases and 140 (8%) controls reported early pregnancy sleep aid use. We calculated aORs for 12/22 defects, which ranged from 0.52 for d-transposition of the great arteries to 1.61 for coarctation of the aorta. All CIs included the null. Results suggest sleep aids do not increase risk of most defects studied, but increased risk for coarctation of the aorta cannot be ruled out. Small numbers limited analyses. Studies examining the severity of underlying sleep disorders and impacts of specific sleep aids would be beneficial.
authors: Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS

papers.title: Epileptiform Discharges in Seizure-Free Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and the Role of Antiseizure Medications.
papers.abstract: To determine the frequency of epileptiform discharges (EPDs) in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) without clinical seizures, assess autism severity using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS-2), and reassess the children after treatment with antiseizure medications (ASMs). A prospective cohort study. Place and Duration of the Study: Four autism centres in Duhok City, Kurdistan Region, Iraq, from August 2024 to August 2025. Fifty children with seizure-free ASD (aged 2.5-18 years) underwent clinical evaluation, electroencephalography (EEG) recording, and severity assessment using CARS-2. Children with EPDs were offered ASMs according to EEG pattern and clinical profile. EEG and CARS-2 assessments were repeated after 6 months. Data were analysed using SPSS version 31.0. Descriptive statistics were presented as means ± standard deviations for continuous variables and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. For group comparisons, independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for small samples were used. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. EPDs were detected in 24 participants (48%). EPDs were focal in 19 cases (79.16) and generalised in 5 cases (20.83). Adherence to ASMs after 6 months was observed in 9 cases (37.5 %). All adherent participants demonstrated EEG improvement and significant reductions in total CARS-2 scores (p = 0.001). Improvements were also observed in the following domains: emotional response (p = 0.023), body use (p = 0.024), activity level (p = 0.026), visual response (p = 0.040), taste, smell and touch (p = 0.057), and general impression of ASD (p = 0.026). Adverse effects were reported in 6/15 (40%) participants whom started ASMs, primarily behavioural. EPDs are common in children with ASD, even in the absence of clinical seizures. When ASMs were used consistently, EEG improvements were observed, and ASD severity scores on the CARS-2 were reduced. Key Words: Anti-seizure medications, Autism spectrum disorder, Electroencephalography, Epileptiform discharges.
papers.journal: Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan : JCPSP

papers.title: Association Between Body Mass Index and Sleep-Related Outcomes in Patients with Cardiovascular Disease.
papers.abstract: To determine the association between body mass index (BMI) and sleep-related outcomes in patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD). A cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Family Medicine Clinic, Ankara Training and Research Hospital, Ankara, Turkiye, from November 2024 to February 2025. A total of 250 patients aged 18-65 years with CVD were included. Data regarding sociodemographic features, chronic conditions, and subjective sleep patterns of the participants were collected. Sleep quality was assessed using the NoSAS score and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Patients were categorised according to BMI. Categorical variables were assessed using chi-square analysis. To identify independent factors associated with excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), multivariable logistic regression was used. Statistical significance was set at p <0.05. Among the patients, 19.6% (n = 49) demonstrated EDS, and 67.2% (n = 168) were classified as high risk for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Age (p = 0.044), snoring (p = 0.003), and feeling fatigued upon waking (p = 0.014) were significantly related to obesity. Increasing BMI in participants was found to be linked with EDS (p = 0.012). In multivariable analysis, obesity (OR = 4.47), snoring (OR = 2.34), and abnormal sleep duration (OR = 2.63) were independently associated with EDS. The presence of EDS was higher in obese patients with CVD. A high proportion of the study population was classified as being at high risk of OSA. Snoring and feeling fatigued upon waking were more common among obese individuals. Effective management of CVD in family medicine and preventive healthcare requires close attention to obesity and sleep-related disorders. Key Words: Cardiovascular disease, Excessive daytime sleepiness, Obesity, Obstructive sleep apnoea.
papers.journal: Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan : JCPSP

papers.title: Lifestyle and contextual approaches for sexual dysfunction.
papers.abstract: Sexual dysfunction, encompassing entities like erectile dysfunction, Peyronie's disease, ejaculatory and orgasmic disorders, and female sexual dysfunction, is highly prevalent and substantially impacts quality of life. While medical and surgical treatments have significantly advanced in the last half-century, they may not address underlying causes or contextual elements that contribute to these multifactorial disorders. This perspective synthesizes evidence-based, holistic approaches to prevention and management of sexual dysfunction, emphasizing their role in preserving "Sexspan", the period of life characterized by satisfying sexual function and intimacy. We narratively review high-level evidence connecting two broad domains that support sexual wellness: (1) lifestyle pillars (diet, exercise, sleep, stress reduction) and (2) contextual domains (partner dynamics, mental health, hormonal wellness, and preventive health maintenance). We summarize disorder-specific applications of these domains and highlight emerging evidence integrating digital health, artificial intelligence, and regenerative approaches. Lifestyle and contextual factors influence endothelial health, hormonal balance, and psychological resilience, directly impacting sexual disorders. Mediterranean diet adherence, aerobic and resistance exercise, restorative sleep, and stress reduction each demonstrate measurable improvements in sexual outcomes across sexes. Partner-inclusive counseling and treatment, mental health care, hormonal assessment and optimization, and routine preventive screening further strengthen the effectiveness of treatments. Emerging digital tools, including wearables, artificial intelligence, and chatbots, offer precision monitoring and personalized intervention, while regenerative approaches remain investigational. In conclusion, holistic management of sexual dysfunction is evidence-based, broadly accessible, and synergistic with medical and surgical therapies. The integrative concept of Sexspan establishes a measurable framework for patients and sexual medicine practitioners alike.

papers.title: Development, implementation, and evaluation of web-based decision support application for developmental care of preterm infants: a multi-phase study.
papers.abstract: Developmental care is a critical component of high-quality neonatal services for preterm infants. However, variability in gestational age assessment and inconsistencies in translating assessment findings into care practices can compromise developmental outcomes. Digital clinical decision support systems may enhance standardization and improve the quality of neonatal care. This study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate a web-based decision support application based on the Ballard assessment to support gestational age determination and developmental care planning. A multi-phase study was conducted, including development, implementation, and evaluation of a web-based clinical decision support application. The system was developed using the Waterfall model and integrated evidence-based developmental care recommendations linked to gestational age scoring. The evaluation phase employed a quasi-experimental pre-post design in a neonatal intensive care unit in Tehran, Iran. Fifty nurses participated. Developmental care performance was assessed using a validated researcher-developed tool before and eight weeks after implementation. User satisfaction was measured using the Mobile App Rating Scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and paired t-tests, with a significance level of 0.05. Following implementation, nurses' performance improved significantly across all developmental care domains (p < 0.001). The most substantial improvements were observed in gestational age determination (effect size (Cohen's d) = 2.25), protected sleep, and family-centered care domains. Overall developmental care scores increased significantly from pre-test to post-test. User satisfaction scores indicated high acceptability, particularly in information quality and functionality domains. The web-based decision support application was feasible, acceptable, and effective in improving nurses' performance in gestational age assessment, and the quality of developmental care delivery in a real-world neonatal setting. Digital decision support tools may contribute to standardizing neonatal care practices and strengthening evidence-based nursing care for preterm infants.
papers.journal: Archives of public health = Archives belges de sante publique

papers.title: Evaluating the efficacy and safety of melatonin for sleep onset insomnia in children aged 6-12: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is an endogenous hormone that regulates the body's sleep-wake cycles. Due to several clinical trials, it is currently used as an exogenous supplement in pediatric patients who suffer from sleep-onset insomnia (SOI). Consequently, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the evidence for the clinical efficacy of melatonin for SOI in children aged 6-12. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of Melatonin for sleep-onset insomnia in children aged 6-12 by conducting literature searches in PubMed (97), Google Scholar (111), OVID (33), and Web of Science (156) databases. We performed statistical tests using RevMan for meta-analysis. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the I2 statistic. To maintain the validity of the studies, each included study was assessed by the Cochrane Collaboration Risk of Bias (ROB) tool. The outcomes investigated were sleep onset time (SOT), sleep onset latency (SOL), total sleep time (TST), all-cause dropout rates, and adverse-event dropout rates. Three hundred ninety-eight records were identified, and 10 randomized clinical trials met the inclusion criteria. The results demonstrated that melatonin treatment group was associated with an earlier sleep onset time compared with placebo with a mean difference (MD) of -0.48 h (approximately 29 min earlier) (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.93 to -0.02 h, p = 0.04). The heterogeneity between studies was moderate (I2 = 63%). On the other hand, it was noted that there has been noticed there was a remarkable reduction in sleep onset latency with melatonin compared to placebo, with an MD of -0.38 (95% CI: -0.57 to -0.20, p < 0.0001), with high heterogeneity (I2 = 82%). Our study confirmed that melatonin has a marked effect regarding Sleep-onset insomnia in childhood. Therefore, we found there was a statistical and clinical improvement in sleep parameters such as sleep onset time (SOT) and total sleep time (TST) which demonstrated the safety and efficacy of melatonin. However, long-term efficacy and safety need to be addressed, especially in the pediatric population.

papers.title: Cannabis-based medicinal products for post-traumatic stress disorder: a two-year prospective analysis from the UK medical cannabis registry.
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterised by persistent psychological symptoms following exposure to trauma. Cannabis-based medicinal products (CBMPs) have promising therapeutic potential. However, there is a paucity of long-term studies investigating their use. This prospective case series aimed to assess changes in patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and the prevalence of adverse events in patients prescribed CBMPs for PTSD. Patients enrolled on the United Kingdom Medical Cannabis Registry for PTSD were included. Changes in PROMs (Impact of Events Scale-Revised (IES-R), Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS) and EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level questionnaire (EQ-5D-5​L)) were assessed from baseline up to 24 months. In total, 446 patients were included, of which 75.11% (n = 335) were already using cannabis before starting treatment. Mean IES-R, GAD-7, SQS and EQ-5D-5​L scores improved relative to baseline at all follow-up times (p < 0.001). At 24 months, 64.57% (n = 288) of IES-R data were imputed. The mean IES-R fell from 59.58 ± 15.93 at baseline to 36.91 ± 18.56 at 24 months, with 55.38% (n = 247) of patients continuing to meet the DSM-IV threshold for PTSD at 24 months. Seventy-five patients (16.82%) reported at least one adverse event. Of 578 events, 83 (14.36%) were severe, and 2 (0.35%) life-threatening or disabling. In this uncontrolled case series, CBMP treatment was associated with improvements in mean PTSD symptom, anxiety, sleep, and health-related quality of life scores. However, the improvement was concentrated within the first month and then plateaued. The observational design, high attrition, and reliance on imputed data preclude any inference of efficacy or causality.

papers.title: Sex-specific developmental pathways link brain networks, sensory sensitivity, and sleep to adolescent pain.
papers.abstract: Multisite pain during adolescence predicts chronic overlapping pain conditions in adulthood, with females disproportionately affected. Sex-related neurobiological mechanisms underlying multisite pain development, however, remain poorly understood. Leveraging four consecutive years of Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study® data, associations between neural connectivity (ages 9-10) and youth-reported number of painful body regions (ages 12-13) are investigated, considering the intermediary roles of sensory sensitivity and subsequent sleep disturbances: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging connectivity among the salience (SLN), sensorimotor (SMN), and default mode (DMN) networks, is assessed separately for males (N = 2760) and females (N = 2728) and are then used in sex-stratified serial mediation models to test sensory sensitivity and sleep disturbances as mediators of links to pain. At age 12-13, 37% of the sample (54% females) report pain. In females, DMN-SLN connectivity is directly related to multisite pain, independent of mediators (b = 3.82, CI = [0.95-6.69]). In males DMN-SMN connectivity is indirectly associated with pain through sensory hypersensitivity and subsequent sleep disturbances (b = 0.18, CI = [0.04-0.43]). Mid and posterior insula centrality predict pain with sex-specific lateralization patterns. In this cohort study, sex-related neurodevelopmental pain pathways are characterized, potentially identifying targets for early, tailored interventions.

papers.title: Experience modifies the synaptome architecture in the developing and adult mouse brain.
papers.abstract: Synaptome architecture describes the spatiotemporal distribution of highly diverse excitatory synapses throughout the brain. Whether and how this architecture is impacted by experience and sensory input is unknown. We found that environmental enrichment and monocular visual deprivation drive large-scale reconfiguration of excitatory synapse populations in more than one hundred regions of the mouse brain. Different experiences modify distinct subsets of synapse types and subtypes, with patterns aligned with protein turnover rates and connectome architecture. Similarity in experience-dependent reconfiguration during development and adulthood indicates shared mechanisms of synaptome adaptation across the lifespan. Our findings support a population-selection model in which experiences drive adaptation by selectively modifying synapse types and subtypes distributed across the brain. Experience-driven reconfiguration of synaptome architecture shares features with the response to aging, sleep deprivation, brain injury and genetic mutations, supporting a unifying principle of brain adaptation.

papers.title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Biophysical Mechanisms, Neural Effects, and Clinical Translation.
papers.abstract: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation technology capable of targeting both cortical and deep brain structures with millimeter-scale spatial precision. Recent advances in ultrasound hardware, acoustic modeling, neuronavigation, and multimodal imaging have accelerated the field from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward mechanistic investigation and early clinical translation. In parallel, growing evidence from animal and human studies has begun to clarify how ultrasound influences neural activity across cellular, circuit, and systems levels. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in understanding the biophysical mechanisms, neurophysiological effects, and network-level consequences of TUS. We discuss insights from optical imaging, electrophysiology, EEG source imaging, and functional MRI, highlighting how these complementary approaches reveal cell-type-specific responses, bidirectional modulation of neural circuits, and distributed changes in functional connectivity beyond the sonicated target. We further examine evidence that functional imaging is evolving from a simple measure of regional activation to a multidimensional biomarker of target engagement, circuit modulation, and treatment response. Despite these advances, important challenges remain. We conclude that TUS is approaching a translational inflection point in which rigorous mechanistic studies, standardized methodologies, and imaging-based biomarkers can establish ultrasound as both a powerful causal neuroscience tool and a clinically viable neuromodulation therapy for disorders involving dysfunctional brain circuits.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

papers.title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
papers.abstract: The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

papers.title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
papers.abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD.Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

papers.title: Anti-immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule 5 disease presenting with severe daytime somnolence and sleep-wake dysregulation.
Sleep quality and depression in patients with cancer receiving chemotherapy: a prospective observational study at a university hospital in Thailand.
Molecular Imaging for Epilepsy Localization and Treatment Planning.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is among the most common neurologic disorders. Obtaining the best possible seizure control is important for quality of life. Frequently, epilepsy is resistant to medication, in about one-third of cases, and surgical evaluation is warranted. Optimal surgical outcomes depend on accurate localization of the epileptogenic zone. Nuclear brain imaging studies provide functional and molecular data that can be crucial in the identifying of epileptogenic areas of the brain. Brain imaging data obtained from perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and interictal PET and PET/MR imaging can inform invasive monitoring with stereotactic electroencephalography and guide the performance of destructive surgical interventions.

papers.title: Inflammation and Integrative Primary Care.
papers.abstract: This article frames inflammation as a central, modifiable driver of chronic disease affecting body, mind, and environment. While acute inflammation is necessary, dysregulated low-grade chronic inflammation contributes to cardiovascular disease, diabetes, asthma, gut disorders, dementia, and mental illness. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is highlighted as a practical clinical marker. Beyond medications, the article emphasizes upstream, lifestyle-based interventions-anti-inflammatory nutrition, physical activity, stress regulation, sleep, social connection, and environmental health. Evidence across major conditions supports integrative, trauma-informed, and equity-aware approaches, underscoring primary care's role in calming the fire of inflammation to improve long-term health outcomes.

papers.title: Botanical Medicines in Primary Care: Foundations of Systems-Based Integrative Practice.
papers.abstract: Primary care clinicians are increasingly caring for patients seeking natural, preventive, and integrative approaches to health. Botanical medicines can serve as evidence-informed and generally well-tolerated tools for addressing common concerns such as stress-related symptoms, poor sleep, gastrointestinal complaints, fatigue, and early metabolic imbalance. Historically, plants were selected based on physiologic patterns-such as depletion, excess, or dysregulation, rather than isolated symptoms. This article reintroduces botanical medicine through a systems-based perspective, integrating traditional pattern recognition with contemporary clinical evidence. Practical clinical guidance is provided for pattern recognition, botanical selection, safety screening, and product-quality considerations to support responsible prescribing in primary care.

papers.title: Beyond Survival: A Systems-Integrated Approach to Clinical Self-Care in Primary Care.
papers.abstract: Primary care clinician burnout is rising and is driven not only by individual stress, but also by structural inefficiency, workplace culture, and moral distress that limits clinicians' ability to deliver value-aligned care. This article reframes clinical self-care as a professional competency and patient safety imperative, grounded in integrative and salutogenic principles. It proposes a systems-integrated Swiss cheese prevention model with 3 aligned layers: (1) structural safeguards (workload/panel size, team-based care, and inbox time), (2) a culture of psychological and moral safety (leadership, dialogue, and peer support), and (3) embedded individual skills (sleep, boundaries, and mind-body regulation).

papers.title: Sleep Health.
papers.abstract: Sleep health is essential for overall health and requires a comprehensive approach. In addition to addressing primary sleep conditions, assessing the physiologic, environmental, behavioral, medical/psychiatric psychosocial, and socioeconomic factors that may affect sleep and wakefulness is important. Comprehensive approaches that include biomedical and integrative treatments can support sleep health. Integrative approaches have been best explored in insomnia, with an opportunity for further research in other sleep conditions such as sleep apnea and restless legs syndrome.

papers.title: Gut-brain-muscle axis in patients with Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), their caregivers, and clinicians encounter a range of motor and non-motor symptoms. The motor symptoms can affect the extremities, trunk, orofacial region, and pharyngolaryngeal structures, whereas the non-motor symptoms include such features as cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, sleep disturbance, autonomic nervous dysregulation, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The diversity and interplay of these symptoms make PD one of the most challenging neurodegenerative diseases to manage. Because multiple symptom domains are simultaneously vulnerable in PD-resembling the multidimensional frailty observed in older adults-maintaining patients' adaptability to daily living is a central therapeutic goal. In this context, we employ the concept of the "gut-brain-muscle axis" as a framework for supporting resilience and mitigating the progression of frailty. This concept emphasizes the bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal system with its microbiota, the central nervous system, and the musculoskeletal system, and highlights how dysfunction in one component can propagate to others, thereby accelerating the progression of frailty. Here, we introduce this concept and discuss how it can be adapted to prevent frailty in PD patients. J. Med. Invest. 73 : 310-318, August, 2026.
papers.journal: The journal of medical investigation : JMI

papers.title: [Epilepsy and Alcohol].
papers.abstract: The association between alcohol consumption and epilepsy is both complex and clinically significant. Acute alcohol intake suppresses central nervous system activity, while abrupt cessation of chronic heavy drinking can trigger rebound neuronal hyperexcitability, resulting in alcohol withdrawal seizures. In patients with epilepsy, heavy or binge drinking may increase seizure risk, particularly when concurrent with sleep deprivation, poor antiseizure medication adherence, dehydration, nutritional disturbances, or metabolic abnormalities. Alcohol-related seizures must be distinguished from alcohol withdrawal seizures, seizures associated with underlying epilepsy, and acute symptomatic seizures attributable to other causes, such as head trauma, cerebrovascular disease, infection, and metabolic disturbances. Therefore, clinical assessments should consider the amount and pattern of alcohol consumption, interval between the last drink and seizure onset, withdrawal symptoms, seizure characteristics, epilepsy history, medication adherence, and other potential precipitants. Benzodiazepines are the mainstay of acute management for alcohol withdrawal seizures, with treatment aiming to control withdrawal syndrome and prevent severe complications, in addition to preventing recurrent seizures. Although heavy alcohol consumption is associated with an increased risk of seizures and epilepsy, evidence regarding the effects of low-level alcohol consumption remains limited. Individualized risk assessment and counseling are essential in clinical practice.
papers.journal: Brain and nerve = Shinkei kenkyu no shinpo

papers.title: Does Montelukast Decrease Post-Adenotonsillectomy Pain in Children? A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness of perioperative Montelukast as an analgesic for adenotonsillectomy. This was a randomized controlled double-blind trial. The trial enrolled 116 children between the age of 3-8 undergoing adenotonsillectomy with planned 23-h observation for sleep disordered breathing were randomized to receive either montelukast or placebo perioperatively. Outcome variables including postoperative opioid usage, FLACC pain scores, post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage rate (PTH), and number of postoperative contacts were examined. One-hundred and thirteen patients received either montelukast or placebo, and 92 received a second dose of the same. There were no differences in demographics between groups. There were no significant differences in the proportion of patients requiring opioids in PACU (46% in control group vs. 45% in the montelukast group, p = 0.9) or the number of postoperative contacts between groups. There was no difference in PTH between groups (p < 0.01). Montelukast does not lead to lower rates of pain postoperatively compared to placebo in patients undergoing adenotonsillectomy for sleep disordered breathing and does not lower postoperative contacts with the medical system. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02793375 LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 2.

papers.title: Individualized and stereotypical seizure semiology in a porcine model of post-traumatic epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Large-animal models of traumatic brain injury may yield translatable data on epileptogenesis, given their similarities in anatomy, brain size, and immune systems to humans. Adult male and female swine received bilateral cortical impact (N = 16) or sham surgery (N = 6) and were screened for convulsions via video-EEG for up to one year. Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) was defined as 2 seizures after 1-week post-injury. Eight out of sixteen pigs (50%) receiving bilateral cortical impact developed PTE, with an average latent period of 5 months (± 3.7). Seizures (N = 190) began focally, sometimes with motor onset including automatisms, before becoming generalized, with tonic-clonic or tonic convulsions. We defined a library differentiating peri-ictal behaviors (N = 31) from rhythmic/odd behaviors typical in healthy pigs (N = 12). Seizures had an average of 6.95 behaviors per seizure (max 26) lasting an average of 1.8 min (max 7.9). For seizures comprised of multiple convulsive episodes, the first convulsion had a greater number of peri-ictal behaviors than subsequent convulsions (P < 0.001). The array of peri-ictal behaviors displayed was moderately pig-specific, with many behaviors consistently observed across seizures. The seizure frequency detected was 0.43/day. This large-brain model of PTE exhibits a variable period of epileptogenesis, a substantial rate of PTE, and an expansive repertoire of ictal behaviors. This first description of semiology in this species will serve as a guide for other porcine epilepsy models. Biofidelic models of PTE are expected to increase our understanding of the pathophysiology, enabling the identification and testing of therapeutics that translate into human patients.

papers.title: Orthographic repetition elicits enhancement without suppression at both the word- and character-levels in Chinese.
papers.abstract: In Chinese, orthographic repetition (e.g., ""-"") modulates neural activity associated with orthographic processing around 200 ms after target onset, as indexed by the N200 enhancement effect. The present study combined time-frequency analysis with priming paradigms in two EEG experiments to determine whether orthographic repetition is accompanied by oscillatory power enhancement or suppression. In Experiment 1, complete repetition priming of two-character words elicited both a significant N200 enhancement effect and significant theta power enhancement relative to the control condition, whereas no significant N200 or theta-power enhancement was detected for semantic or phonological priming. To separate orthographic overlap from the concomitant phonological and semantic repetition inherent in complete repetition, Experiment 2 used partial orthographic repetition with single-character prime-target pairs that differed in phonology and semantics and replicated both effects. Exploratory participant-level correlations between the N200 and total theta effects were positive but nonsignificant in both experiments. A positive correlation between N200 enhancement and evoked theta enhancement reached the unadjusted significance threshold only in Experiment 2. These findings indicate that orthographic repetition is associated with enhancement rather than suppression of theta-band activity and that this pattern extends across word and character levels.
papers.journal: International journal of psychophysiology : official journal of the International Organization of Psychophysiology

papers.title: Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy: Reappraising a Historical Clinical Concept in the Era of Multimodal Imaging.
papers.abstract: Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) and the broader "AZOOR complex" have historically encompassed several disorders sharing acute visual symptoms and outer retinal dysfunction. Advances in multimodal imaging have revealed structural abnormalities in many of these presentations, challenging the original concept of an "occult" retinopathy without a visible anatomical correlate. We therefore revisit these concepts in light of modern imaging and current understanding of outer retinal disease. A systematic reassessment of 207 eligible published cases showed that 188 (90.8%) could be assigned a more specific contemporary diagnostic category based on the information available in the original reports. The most frequent assignments were multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS), acute outer retinopathy (AOR), and multizonal outer retinopathy and retinal pigment epitheliopathy (MORR). These findings do not establish that the original diagnoses were incorrect or that each contemporary diagnosis represents a biologically independent disease, but show that many presentations historically grouped under AZOOR can now be characterized more specifically. We review the clinical features, multimodal imaging findings, natural history, and management of the principal retinal entities identified through this reassessment. We also examine inherited, toxic, autoimmune, paraneoplastic, post-infectious, and other disorders that may produce similar retinal appearances or provide the underlying clinical or etiological setting for these presentations. Rather than proposing a new disease classification, we suggest a pattern-based diagnostic approach in which OCT and fundus autofluorescence form the core imaging assessment, with additional imaging modalities selected according to the clinical presentation and differential diagnosis. Imaging is used to characterize the predominant pattern and anatomical level of retinal injury and, when possible, to identify a more specific retinal diagnosis; clinical history, systemic evaluation, laboratory testing, electrophysiology, and genetic testing can then guide further investigation of its etiological setting or identify a specific alternative diagnosis. This approach allows patients presenting within the broad clinical spectrum historically associated with AZOOR to be characterized at the most specific level supported by contemporary imaging, while recognizing that the biological relationships among these retinal entities remain incompletely understood.
papers.journal: Progress in retinal and eye research

papers.title: Evolutionary patterns and functional consequences of acetylcholinesterase mutations associated with organophosphate resistance in Panonychus citri.
papers.abstract: Organophosphate insecticides (OPs) inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and target-site mutations in the Ace gene represent an important resistance mechanism in arthropod pests. However, the evolutionary origins of such mutations and their functional consequences in field populations remain incompletely resolved. Here, we surveyed three nonsynonymous Ace substitutions, A352S, G480A, and Y483W (corresponding to A201S, G328A, and F331W in Torpedo californica), across 31 P. citri field populations sampled from major citrus-growing regions of China. Fragment-specific haplotype analyses revealed close relationships between resistance-associated and susceptible haplotypes, although the unphased fragments limited the determination of full-length haplotype ancestry. Bioassays and binding analyses showed that these substitutions reduced OP binding and produced modest decreases in susceptibility to chlorpyrifos, profenofos, and phoxim, with the Y483W substitution showing the largest effect. Molecular modelling suggested that Y483W may impair insecticide binding through steric hindrance, whereas A352S and G480A may act through indirect structural effects. Moreover, introduction of the corresponding substitutions into Drosophila revealed pronounced fitness-related effects, including reduced fecundity, lower egg-to-adult viability, shortened lifespan, impaired locomotor performance, diminished heat tolerance, and disrupted circadian activity rhythms. Together, these results link field allele distributions and fragment-specific haplotype relationships with the functional effects of AChE substitutions on organophosphate susceptibility, and provide a basis for further investigating how these resistance-associated alleles are maintained in natural populations.

papers.title: Feedback Processing in Individual and Dyadic Group Risk Decisions Under Gain-Loss Framing: Evidence from FRN and P3b.
papers.abstract: Decision-making in social contexts is influenced by gain-loss framing and interpersonal responsibility, yet how these factors jointly shape the neural dynamics of outcome evaluation remains unclear. Using event-related potentials (ERPs) and a dyadic turn-taking Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), this study examined how decision context (individual vs. dyadic group), gain-loss framing, and feedback valence influence risky choice and feedback processing. Participants completed the task in both individual and dyadic contexts while EEG was recorded. Behaviorally, participants exhibited greater risk-taking in the dyadic group than in the individual context and showed reduced risk-taking following negative relative to positive feedback. ERP analyses revealed significant interactions between decision context and feedback valence for both feedback-related negativity (FRN) and P3b, suggesting that decision context modulated neural responses associated with both early and later stages of outcome evaluation. Specifically, FRN responses to negative feedback were enhanced in the dyadic context, whereas P3b responses were larger in the individual context. The dyadic context also enhanced neural differentiation between positive and negative feedback. In addition, P3b showed a descriptive pattern consistent with a possible interaction between decision context and gain-loss framing, although this interaction did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings demonstrate that social decision context shapes both behavioral risk-taking and the neural dynamics of feedback processing during interactive sequential decision-making. The study extends previous research by providing neurophysiological evidence from a real dyadic interactive paradigm, highlighting how social context influences outcome evaluation under risk.

papers.title: Bimodal versus unimodal high-definition Transcranial random noise stimulation of auditory cortex for tinnitus: A double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial.
papers.abstract: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) targeting auditory cortex has shown preliminary promise for chronic tinnitus, but evidence is dominated by small studies and powered trials are scarce. A single-session pilot suggested that pairing HD-tRNS with acoustic input may augment its effects, whether this holds over repeated sessions is unknown. We investigated whether repeated sessions of HD-tRNS over bilateral auditory cortex, delivered alone or combined with acoustic stimulation, modulate tinnitus loudness, auditory deviant processing, and resting-state connectivity. Thirty-five participants with chronic tinnitus completed a double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial. Participants were assigned to bimodal (HD-tRNS plus acoustic stimulation) or unimodal (HD-tRNS alone) arms, each with active and sham blocks of 10 sessions over bilateral Heschl's gyrus. Outcomes included minimum masking level (MML), visual analogue scales for loudness and distress, mismatch negativity to intensity deviants, and resting-state connectivity. No consistent treatment effect emerged. Bayesian evidence favoured the null for the primary loudness outcome (BF01=4.79), and neither primary mismatch negativity outcome survived correction. For MML, the main treatment effect was null, but an unexpected group × treatment interaction emerged at post (p=0.039), mirrored in connectivity. Repeated HD-tRNS produced no group-level benefit, alone or combined with acoustic stimulation, adding a well-controlled null to a mixed literature.

papers.title: Slow-timescale regulation of dopamine release governs recovery of a motivational drive over days.
papers.abstract: The rise and fall of a motivational state can unfold over many days. We used mouse mating behavior to model how the brain orchestrates such slow-timescale changes in motivation. Male mice become sexually satiated after successful matings, and their motivation to mate recovers over a week. Using deep-brain fluorescence-lifetime imaging in the medial preoptic area (MPOA), we found that tonic dopamine transmission-which regulates mating drive-also declined after mating and gradually re-emerged across several days. Two mechanisms regulated dopamine transmission. First, successful mating transiently reduced the tonic firing of hypothalamic dopamine-releasing neurons, thereby inhibiting dopamine release and mating behavior for 1 to 2 days. Second, these neurons' ability to produce and release dopamine dropped after mating and recovered over the following week, paralleling the recovery of mating drive. Therefore, changes in neuronal firing rate and neurotransmitter composition cooperate to control the early and late phases of motivational dynamics, respectively.

papers.title: Timing the feast: Circadian control of rhizosphere nitrogen supply.
papers.abstract: The challenge of nitrogen use efficiency stems from a "handshake" problem between soil supply and plant demand. In this issue, Du and colleagues reveal how the rice circadian regulator Nhd1 uses rhythmic chemical signals to synchronize microbial nitrogen cycling with plant uptake and assimilation, providing an example of "chronoculture."

papers.title: Design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of novel Nav1.2 inhibitors as antiepileptic agents.
papers.abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2 is a validated target for anticonvulsant therapy, yet Nav1.2 inhibitors remain scarce. To explore the unexplored N-4 position of the [1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine scaffold, we designed and synthesized two series of novel derivatives bearing diverse substituents at this position. Their Nav1.2 inhibitory activities were evaluated using FLIPR membrane potential and whole-cell patch-clamp assays, while their anticonvulsant efficacy and neurotoxicity were assessed in MES/ sc-PTZ seizure models and rotarod test, respectively. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis revealed that hydrophobic volume complementarity, rather than aromaticity, is the primary driver of Nav1.2 potency. Compound 3b, bearing a simple n-butyl group at N-4, emerged as the most promising lead, exhibiting moderate Nav1.2 inhibition (88.9% at 30 μM; FLIPR IC50 = 11.55 μM; patch-clamp IC50 = 7.62 μM for the inactivated state) and exceptional in vivo efficacy (ED50 = 9.17 mg/kg, TD50 > 813.40 mg/kg, PI >88.70) in the sc-PTZ model. Compound 3y also demonstrated moderate Nav1.2 inhibition (69.8%, IC50 = 12.19 μM) and potent anticonvulsant activity (ED50 = 13.7 mg/kg, PI >23.1). Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed that 3b and 3y inhibit the inactivated state of Nav1.2 (IC50 = 7.62 μM and 8.31 μM, respectively) with negligible effect on the resting state. Molecular docking and MD simulations revealed that 3b binds within the Nav1.2 pore via hydrogen bonds, π-π stacking, and hydrophobic contacts. Tissue distribution studies demonstrated efficient blood-brain barrier penetration (brain-to-plasma ratio of 1.65 at 1 h post-dose). Although 3b showed limited stability in human and rat liver microsomes (T1/2 = 12.20 and 10.65 min, respectively), its potent in vivo efficacy and exceptionally high protective index support its continued optimization and preclinical development as a promising candidate for epilepsy therapy.

papers.title: Sleep quality, age, and sex on intrinsic brain networks.
Sleep disturbance and anxiety in female garment workers with tinnitus: An ENT outpatient study.
papers.abstract: Tinnitus distress often coexists with poor sleep and anxiety. Plausible links run through sleep fragmentation at night, emotional load and reduced prefrontal regulation of the auditory signal, but the direction of these associations is unsettled. Female ready-made garment (RMG) workers in Bangladesh work long shifts in noisy factories, and no published study has measured these three outcomes together in this group. We conducted a cross-sectional analytical study, reported according to STROBE, at an ENT outpatient clinic in Baipail, Savar, Bangladesh, between May 2025 and April 2026. One hundred and twenty female RMG workers with subjective tinnitus completed the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), and underwent pure-tone audiometry. Spearman correlations were the primary measure of association. Stepwise multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, employment duration, daily working hours, department, income, marital status, 4 kHz threshold and tinnitus duration. Sensitivity analyses used logistic regression and a normal-hearing subgroup. Mean age was 29.5 ± 8.0 years. High-frequency sensorineural hearing loss was present in 63.3% of workers and a 4 kHz notch in 58.3%. Poor sleep (PSQI >5) affected 72.5% and moderate-to-severe anxiety 65.0%. THI correlated with PSQI (ρ = 0.65, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.74) and GAD-7 (ρ = 0.70, 0.60 to 0.78). After full adjustment, each 10-point rise in THI was associated with 1.14 points higher PSQI (0.93 to 1.35) and 1.33 points higher GAD-7 (1.07 to 1.59). The odds ratios per 10 THI points were 2.61 (1.68 to 4.05) for poor sleep and 2.53 (1.71 to 3.73) for moderate-to-severe anxiety. The 4 kHz threshold was not associated with either outcome. In this cohort, tinnitus handicap was independently associated with worse sleep and greater anxiety, while audiometric severity was not.

papers.title: Electrophysiological evidence for altered cognitive control processes in the prodromal phase of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP) is a neurodegenerative movement disorder caused by a mutation in the TAF1 gene, characterized by early striatal pathology. While cognitive alterations have been described in manifest XDP, little is known about the prodromal phase. To pinpoint electrophysiological signatures of cognitive control in male non-manifesting carriers of the XDP-causing mutation (NMC) 14 genetically confirmed NMC and 36 healthy controls (HC) completed a combined flanker/stop-signal task while EEG was recorded. Event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with performance monitoring and response inhibition were analyzed. While behavioral performance and inhibitory control were comparable between groups, NMCs exhibited a significantly enhanced correct-related negativity (CRN) revealing an electrophysiological signature of enhanced internal performance monitoring while behavioral and inhibitory control is preserved. This CRN enhancement may reflect early functional alterations in fronto-striatal networks and provides first neurophysiological evidence of changed executive function in prodromal XDP, supporting a staged model of cognitive involvement preceding motor symptom onset. The findings of this proof-of-concept study, however, require independent confirmation.

papers.title: Healthy aging, processing speed, and mnemonic brain state engagement.
papers.abstract: Healthy older adults exhibit both selective impairments in episodic memory - memory for events situated within a specific time and place - and deficits in executive function, reflected by difficulty switching between different tasks and inhibiting task-irrelevant information. Prior work has shown that older adults show diminished mnemonic brain state engagement - recruitment of whole brain activity patterns that selectively support memory encoding and memory retrieval. Our hypothesis is that older adults are biased toward the retrieval state and, due to executive function deficits, cannot easily switch out of this state when task-irrelevant. Our goal was to determine the extent to which stimulus processing time impacts older adult mnemonic state engagement, with the expectation that longer processing times would enable older adults to switch out of a task-irrelevant retrieval state. We recorded scalp electroencephalography (EEG) while younger and older adult participants explicitly encoded and retrieved object stimuli under variable stimulus durations. Using a combination of multivariate decoding approaches, we find that under time constraints, older adults both under-recruit a young adult-like retrieval state when task-relevant, but over-recruit a participant-specific retrieval state when task-irrelevant. Older adults may thus recruit idiosyncratic activity patterns to compensate for difficulties engaging young adult-like mnemonic brain states. Taken together, these findings suggest that although older adults retain the ability to engage encoding and retrieval brain states, they require more processing time to both initiate and maintain goal-relevant mnemonic states.

papers.title: Drug-resistant epilepsy in non-NF1 RASopathies: a two-centre retrospective paediatric cohort and scoping review.
