papers.abstract: We evaluated 11 male workers with elevated serum manganese levels and T1 hyperintensities in the globus pallidus, features of manganese toxicity, all of whom were employed at a single ferromanganese plant. They exhibited clinical features of manganism, including behavioral issues, forgetfulness, headache, decreased sleep, generalized weakness, tingling and stretching sensations in the limbs, hand and jaw tremors, dysarthria, hypophonia, rapid speech, rigidity, difficulty in walking, and falls. Positron emission tomography scans performed on two patients showed presynaptic dopaminergic deficits. All patients ceased working in the environment and experienced partial improvement with levodopa therapy.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology

papers.title: Acute intermittent carotid body stimulations induce long-term facilitation of respiratory-cardiovascular coupling in rats.
papers.abstract: Hypertension, the leading modifiable risk factor for global mortality, is driven in >50% of cases by neurogenic mechanisms linked to heightened sympathetic nerve activity (SNA). A hallmark of neurogenic hypertension is the exacerbation of respiratory-modulated SNA (RespSNA) and resulting blood pressure Traube-Hering (TH) waves, which emerges during the prehypertensive period and contributes to disease development. Carotid bodies (CBs), the peripheral chemoreceptors involved in the hypoxic response, are hyperactive in hypertensive patients and animal models. Their chronic intermittent stimulation, as seen in obstructive sleep apnoea, promotes hypertension characterised by exacerbated RespSNA and TH waves. Yet, their causal role in initiating these changes remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether acute intermittent CB stimulations could directly enhance RespSNA, TH waves and blood pressure from a physiological baseline, using the in situ working heart-brainstem preparation in rats. Four brief CB stimulations with sodium cyanide, mimicking acute intermittent hypoxia, were sufficient to induce a prolonged (>20 min) increase in both inspiratory and late expiratory RespSNA bursts, TH waves and perfusion pressure, with these effects being prevented by carotid sinus denervation. These changes were accompanied by a reconfiguration of central respiratory and cardiovascular control, including elevated respiratory heart rate variability and enhanced respiratory drive targeting upper airway and abdominal muscles. Our findings demonstrate that acute intermittent CB activation triggers sustained RespSNA and elevation of TH waves, supporting its potential role in development of hypertension. Our data also suggest that CBs play a key role in initiating this respiratory-cardiovascular plasticity and that central mechanisms might contribute to its long-term maintenance. KEY POINTS: Carotid body (CB) overactivity is implicated in sympathetic excitation and development of hypertension, but its direct role in initiating respiratory-cardiovascular dysfunction remains unresolved. We tested whether brief, repeated CB stimulations could trigger lasting changes in breathing and blood pressure control from a physiological baseline. In rats, only four stimulations induced a persistent increase in respiratory-modulated sympathetic activity, elevating blood pressure fluctuations (Traube-Hering waves) and mean blood pressure. These effects, prevented by carotid sinus denervation, were linked to enhanced respiratory-cardiovascular coupling and altered upper airway and abdominal motor control. Our findings reveal that short-term CB activation can induce long-term facilitation of respiratory-cardiovascular coupling, relevant to both physiological adaptations and hypertension pathogenesis.

papers.title: [Post-traumatic growth in male erectile dysfunction patients: The role of family function, fear of disease progression and self-perceived burden].
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this study is to investigate the current status of post-traumatic growth (PTG) in male erectile dysfunction （ED） patients, and to analyze the mediating effects of self-perceived burden and family functioning on the fear of disease progression's chain-mediated impact on PTG. Methods A total of 386 male ED patients admitted to the Second Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University between June 2023 and December 2024 were selected as research subjects. The study employed questionnaires including the General Information Questionnaire, International Erectile Dysfunction Index (IIEF), Family Caregiving Index (APGAR), Post-Traumatic Growth Index (PTGI), Simplified Fear of Disease Progression Scale (FoP-Q-SF) and Self-Perceived Burden Scale (SPBS). Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess relationships among PTG, self-perceived burden, family functioning and fear of disease progression. While structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted using Amos 21.0 software to evaluate mediating effects. Results Among 386 male ED patients, the Patient-Reported Global Score (PTG) scored （51.37±7.24）, family function （8.21±1.12）, fear of disease progression （35.28±5.31）, and self-perceived burden （32.56±5.26）. Age, shame, chronic diseases, cultural factors, social stress and sleep quality were statistically significant predictors for PTG (P<0.05). PTG showed positive correlations with family function and fear of disease progression, but negative correlations with self-perceived burden (all P<0.05). Family function exhibited significant negative correlations with both fear of disease progression and self-perceived burden (P<0.01). Fear of disease progression and self-reported burden demonstrated positive correlations (P<0.05). The study confirmed a chain mediation effect of family function on PTG, with the total indirect effect accounting for 34.23% of the total effect. Specifically, the specific mediation effect of fear of disease progression accounted for 16.99%, self-perceived burden for 14.25%, and the combined chain mediation effect for 2.99%. Conclusion The chain mediation effect between fear of disease progression, self-perceived burden, family function and PTG was established in male erectile dysfunction patients. This confirms that family function can influence PTG by moderating the levels of fear of disease progression and self-perceived burden.
papers.journal: Zhonghua nan ke xue = National journal of andrology
keywords: erectile dysfunction; post-traumatic growth; family functioning; fear of disease progression; self-perceived burden

papers.title: Invasive Monitoring in Acute Liver Failure.
papers.abstract: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rapidly progressive condition marked by severe hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy, and high short-term mortality driven largely by cerebral edema and circulatory collapse. Because neurological deterioration and hemodynamic instability can evolve unpredictably and interact dynamically, continuous physiologic monitoring is central to management. Invasive intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring provides the most direct assessment of intracranial dynamics and supports cerebral perfusion pressure-oriented therapy; however, its routine use remains controversial due to limited outcome data and substantial hemorrhagic risk in the setting of severe coagulopathy. Current evidence, largely observational, favors a selective approach to ICP monitoring in patients with advanced encephalopathy or rapidly worsening neurological status, particularly in experienced centers. Noninvasive adjuncts, including optic nerve sheath ultrasound, transcranial Doppler, and electroencephalography, offer complementary information but do not replace direct ICP measurement. Hemodynamic monitoring, anchored by continuous arterial pressure measurement and central venous access, is indispensable for maintaining systemic perfusion and protecting cerebral blood flow. Advanced cardiac output monitoring and echocardiography further enable individualized fluid and vasopressor strategies. Overall, a multimodal, physiology-driven monitoring framework that integrates neurological and circulatory assessment is essential to optimize outcomes in ALF.

papers.title: Exploring the role of nicotine and smoking in sleep behaviours: A multi-variable Mendelian randomisation study.
papers.abstract: Increased nicotine exposure (resulting from greater cigarette consumption and/or slower nicotine metabolism) may directly affect sleep and could underlie relationships between smoking and sleep behaviours identified previously. We conducted a Mendelian randomisation (MR) study to explore whether nicotine metabolism has a causal effect on sleep behaviours. Our main analysis method was inverse-variance weighted (IVW) Multivariable MR, which was used to examine the independent effects of nicotine metabolism and smoking heaviness on sleep behaviours. The model was developed to provide insights into the potential role of nicotine exposure. The genome-wide association summary data for these analyses were sourced from published genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary-level data, or GWAS conducted within the UK Biobank. Primary analyses focused on current smokers of European descent (N = 5185 to 487 153). We used genetic proxies of the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR), cigarettes per day (CPD), and sleep behaviours (chronotype [being an "evening" person versus a "morning" person], ease of getting up in the morning, insomnia symptoms, napping, daytime sleepiness and sleep duration). Higher NMR (consistent with lower circulating nicotine levels per cigarette smoked) decreased the likelihood of being an "evening" person when accounting for CPD in current smokers [beta coefficient (β) = -0.04, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.06 to -0.02, p < 0.001]. A higher NMR also increased the ease of getting up (β = 0.02, 95%CI 0.01 to 0.04, p = 0.001) and likelihood of napping (β = 0.02, 95%CI 0.01 to 0.03, p < 0.001) in current smokers. There was no consistent evidence for effects of NMR or CPD on insomnia symptoms or sleep duration, although increased sleep duration lowered NMR among current smokers (β = -0.43, 95%CI -0.74 to -0.12, p = 0.007), without corresponding effects on smoking heaviness. Among current smokers, nicotine metabolism may play a direct role in the relationship between smoking and certain sleep behaviours, particularly those related to circadian preference and daytime alertness, independent of smoking heaviness. There is some evidence that sleep duration may influence nicotine metabolism.

papers.title: Cardiovascular Health Promotion for US Veterans: Current State, Gaps, and Strategies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
papers.abstract: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation's largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non-Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.
authors: American Heart Association Council on Lifestyle and Cardiometabolic Health; Council on Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis and Vascular Biology; Council on Cardiovascular and Stroke Nursing; Council on Cardiovascular Radiology and Intervention; Council on Clinical Cardiology; and Council on Quality of Care and Outcomes Research
keywords: United States Department of Veterans Affairs

papers.title: Structurally related Ca2+-release activated Ca2+ channel inhibitors exhibit distinct extracellular and intracellular modes of action.
papers.abstract: Ca2+-release activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels, formed by stromal interaction molecule (STIM) and Orai proteins, mediate store-operated Ca2+ entry and are implicated in autoimmune diseases, acute pancreatitis and cancer. Some small molecule inhibitors of these channels such as BTP2, Pyr6, Synta66 and GSK-7975A, are widely used as experimental tools, yet their precise mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood. Using whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology in rat basophilic leukaemia (RBL-1) cells, we determined whether each of these inhibitors acts from the extracellular or intracellular side of the plasma membrane. We found that BTP2 and GSK-7975A could suppress CRAC currents only when applied extracellularly, whereas Pyr6 and Synta66 were equally effective from either side. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations using a rat Orai1 channel model identified plausible extracellular binding sites for all four inhibitors and additional putative intracellular binding sites for Pyr6 and Synta66. These predicted sites are located near regions that are likely to influence pore geometry and channel gating. Our findings suggest that, despite considerable structural similarity, these popular CRAC channel inhibitors exhibit mechanistically distinct interactions with Orai1, with important implications for their use as research tools and for future CRAC channel drug discovery.

papers.title: The Missing Temporal Coordinate: A Framework for Biopsy Timestamping and Chrono-Biobanking in Precision Oncology and Longevity Medicine.
papers.abstract: Precision medicine increasingly relies on biospecimen analysis for diagnosis, prognostic assessment, treatment selection, and longitudinal monitoring. Established biobanking frameworks address collection methods, processing delays, fixation, and storage. Collection times may also be recorded, but documentation may be inconsistent, and timestamps may not be retained in research datasets or considered in subsequent analyses. Because several physiological processes vary across the day, sampling time may provide relevant context for interpreting selected molecular and cellular measurements. In oncology, circadian regulation influences immune cell distribution, endocrine signaling, metabolism, and gene expression. Sampling time may therefore contribute to variability in selected blood-based biomarkers and molecular profiles. However, the magnitude and clinical relevance of these effects differ across analytes, tissues, and clinical settings and remain insufficiently characterized for many routinely used biomarkers. Similar considerations apply to geroscience and longevity medicine, where some measurements arise from systems with daily variation. Whether this variability meaningfully affects specific epigenetic clocks, biological age estimators, or assessments of intervention response requires direct validation. This narrative review examines evidence relevant to the temporal context of biospecimen collection and proposes a practical framework for timestamping and chrono-biobanking. Proposed core metadata include the local collection date and time, the applicable time zone or UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) offset when available, specimen type, anatomical site, and clearly distinguished processing timestamps. Additional information on fasting, medications, treatment exposure, sleep, and chronotype may be recorded according to the clinical or research question. Comparable collection windows may be useful for serial sampling when feasible and scientifically justified. The proposed framework prioritizes systematic documentation within existing workflows. Integration with electronic health records, laboratory systems, and biobank databases could facilitate the capture and preservation of collection times without delaying necessary care. These data may support temporal stratification, sensitivity analyses, and statistical adjustment where study design and data permit. The framework's feasibility and its effect on biomarker interpretation require empirical evaluation. Preserving sampling-time information provides a foundation for investigating its relevance to biomarker reproducibility and interpretation in precision oncology and longevity research.

papers.title: Probable HHV-6 Limbic Encephalitis after Liver Transplantation: Diagnostic Overlap with Tacrolimus Neurotoxicity and Refractory Status Epilepticus.
papers.abstract: Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) encephalitis is an uncommon but severe post-transplant complication. A 64-year-old woman developed confusion, behavioural changes, and staring episodes 6 months after liver transplantation. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) multiplex testing was positive for HHV-6, and magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral hippocampal and mesial temporal abnormalities, later involving the bitemporal and insular regions. Her course was complicated by refractory status epilepticus, cardiac arrest, kidney injury, prolonged ventilation, pancytopenia, recurrent HHV-6 positivity, and death. This case highlights the challenge of interpreting CSF HHV-6 positivity amid competing diagnoses and the treatment burden imposed by antiviral and antiseizure drug toxicity. Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) limbic encephalitis should remain an important diagnostic consideration in solid organ transplant recipients presenting with otherwise unexplained encephalopathy or temporal-lobe seizures, even months after transplantation and without a classic meningoencephalitic presentation.A positive cerebrospinal fluid HHV-6 result should not be interpreted in isolation. Internists should integrate the clinical syndrome, magnetic resonance imaging distribution, electroencephalogram findings, immunosuppression, and competing diagnoses such as tacrolimus neurotoxicity when determining whether HHV-6 is pathogenic.Management may be as challenging as diagnosis: probable severe HHV-6 limbic encephalitis can require prolonged antiviral and antiseizure therapy, while nephrotoxicity, marrow suppression, bradycardia, and hepatic dysfunction may substantially limit treatment and require repeated reassessment.
papers.journal: European journal of case reports in internal medicine

papers.title: Physical Wellbeing Scavenger Hunt.
papers.abstract: This small group session is appropriate for any level of medical student, emergency medicine resident physicians, and faculty. Burnout is a major issue in medicine, with over half of physicians experiencing burnout at some point in their career.1 Physicians who regularly participate in self-care activities, such as regularly exercising, having a well-balanced diet, and appropriate amount of sleep, experience less burnout.2,3,4 As a resident, it is difficult to find time to practice self-care.2 This session sought to combine education on how to implement appropriate self-care as a trainee and how to carry that forward after training in a way that was fun, provided a period of physical exercise, and provided time outdoors for those participating. By the end of this session, the learner will be able to: 1) implement basic ways to improve sleep quality, 2) avoid common pitfalls in diet and nutrition, 3) incorporate more physical activity into their lives. Learners were divided into teams of three to four. A scavenger hunt was created using Google Forms and QR codes. The initial QR code was displayed in the lecture hall at the start of the session. Fifteen other QR codes were either physically distributed throughout the Emergency Medicine Offices and the Emergency Department or provided to participants via text message when they completed certain tasks. Each QR code led to a different Google Form with a question about physical wellbeing. Participants were allowed to use any resource they had with them, including their mobile devices. After the question was answered correctly, an explanation was provided in the Google Form. A riddle was also provided to help locate the next QR code. An incorrect answer required the participants to try to answer the question again. Participants were not given any hints after answering incorrectly. There were no formal penalties for incorrect answers. However, incorrect answers increased the time it took to complete the task. At the end of the session, each question was debriefed by the instructor. Participants completed a five-question pre-survey to rate their level of physical wellbeing using a 1-5 Likert Scale. Participants also completed a 10-question post survey that asked them the same initial 5 questions to rate their physical wellbeing on the same scale as the pretest, as well as additional questions asking how likely they were to change their physical habits based on the session and how much they enjoyed the session on a different 1-5 Likert Scale. They were also asked to provide recommendations for future changes. Pre- and post-test Likert scores were compared using the Mann-Whitney U Test. Twelve participants, all resident physicians, took part in the exercise. Twelve completed the pre-survey, and ten completed the post-survey. There was no difference in physical wellbeing score (median 3 before vs median 2.5 after, P=0.62). All participants except one were at least moderately likely (3 or above on a 1-5 Likert scale) to change their sleep habits based on the exercise. All were at least moderately likely (3 or above on a 1-5 Likert scale) to change their eating and exercise habits based on the activity. All respondents found the activity to be at least moderately enjoyable (3 or above), with 8 of 10 finding it extremely enjoyable (5). This wellbeing scavenger hunt effectively taught learners how to incorporate simple changes into their lives to improve the self-care habits. This model could be applied to other educational topics to incorporate a component of physical wellbeing and exercise and has been used during new resident orientation and wilderness education within our department. Wellbeing, physical wellbeing, exercise, nutrition, sleep habits, self-care.
papers.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

papers.title: Problematic smartphone use and usage metrics: A comparison of subjective and objective measures among medical students.
papers.abstract: Research on problematic smartphone use (PSU) relies on self-reported screen time as a proxy for severity, despite concerns regarding its utility. Objective usage metrics remain underutilized. To estimate PSU prevalence among medical students and explore screen time's utility as a severity indicator by comparing subjective and objective measures. Associations with selected psychological variables examined. This cross-sectional study included 200 randomly selected undergraduate medical students from a government medical college in Kerala. PSU was assessed using the Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version. Depressive symptoms, perceived stress, mindfulness, and sleep quality were measured using PHQ-9, PSS-10, FFMQ-15, and PSQI. Objective metrics included daily screen time and unlock frequency from in-built tracking applications. Correlation and exploratory regression analyses were performed. Participants underestimated smartphone use compared with objective screen time, with greater underestimation at higher usage levels (P < 0.001). Neither subjective nor objective screen time independently associated with PSU severity. Unlock frequency showed small associations with depressive symptoms and stress. Depression, not screen time, was associated with severity (β = 0.423, P < 0.001). Overall, 26% (95% CI: 20.1-32.7%) were classified as higher-risk. In a study designed to estimate the prevalence of problematic smartphone use, total screen time, whether self-reported or objectively recorded, showed limited utility as a standalone severity indicator, whereas depressive symptoms demonstrated the strongest independent association with PSU.

papers.title: Prevalence of Overweight and Obesity and Their Associations With Screen Time and Other Behavioral Factors Among Adolescents in the United Arab Emirates.
papers.abstract: Background Overweight and obesity among adolescents are major public health concerns. Sociodemographic, familial, dietary, and lifestyle factors, including screen time and physical activity, may be associated with excess body weight. In the United Arab Emirates (UAE), limited evidence has examined recreational screen time alongside these factors in the same adolescent population. Objective This study aimed to determine the prevalence of overweight and obesity among adolescents aged 14-18 years in the UAE and examine whether greater recreational screen time was associated with higher odds of overweight/obesity. Secondary analyses assessed associations of sociodemographic, familial, dietary, physical activity, and sleep factors with overweight/obesity. Methodology A cross-sectional study included 688 adolescents aged 14-18 years recruited from participating high schools and a university teaching hospital in the UAE between December 2023 and April 2024. Height and weight were measured by the investigators, and BMI was classified using sex- and age-specific WHO 2007 growth reference cutoffs. Participants completed a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, family history, dietary habits, physical activity, screen time, and sleep. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression. Results The prevalence of combined overweight/obesity was 39.8% (95% CI: 36.2-43.5%); 27.3% (95% CI: 24.0-30.7%) were overweight, and 12.5% (95% CI: 10.0-15.0%) were obese. Although weekend non-academic screen time was associated with overweight/obesity in the chi-square analysis (p = 0.017), no screen-time category was significant in bivariable logistic regression. In multivariable analysis, overweight/obesity was associated with male sex (AOR = 1.636, 95% CI: 1.155-2.318; p = 0.006), family history of obesity (AOR = 2.014, 95% CI: 1.197-3.389; p = 0.008), frequent eating when not hungry or bored (AOR = 1.884, 95% CI: 1.012-3.509; p = 0.046), and no participation in ≥60 minutes/day of out-of-school moderate-to-vigorous physical activity on any day of the week (AOR = 1.896, 95% CI: 1.285-2.799; p = 0.001). Conclusions Overweight and obesity were common among adolescents in this study. Recreational screen time was not associated with overweight/obesity in the regression analysis. Male gender, family history of obesity, frequent eating when not hungry or bored, and no participation in ≥60 minutes/day of out-of-school moderate-to-vigorous physical activity were associated with overweight/obesity after adjustment. Given the cross-sectional design and recruitment from participating schools and a university teaching hospital, these findings represent associations rather than causal relationships and are not nationally representative of UAE adolescents.
keywords: childhood obesity in the united arab emirates

papers.title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
papers.abstract: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort. Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score). Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed. Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

papers.title: RhinAsthma Patient Perspective: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Validation of a Brief Rhinitis and Asthma Quality-of-Life Measure in Chinese Adults.
papers.abstract: Combined allergic rhinitis and asthma syndrome (CARAS) impairs health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The 8-item RhinAsthma Patient Perspective (RAPP) measures their combined impact. We translated and culturally adapted the RAPP for China and evaluated its psychometric properties. Following International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research principles, the RAPP was translated from Italian into simplified Chinese and cognitively debriefed. Psychometric evaluation included 164 adults with comorbid allergic rhinitis and asthma; 80 with isolated allergic rhinitis and 80 with isolated asthma served as exploratory comparators. Internal consistency, 2-week test-retest reliability, structural, convergent, and discriminant validity, 4-week responsiveness, sex-related differential item functioning (DIF), item response theory (IRT) characteristics, and feasibility were evaluated. In participants with both conditions, responsiveness was assessed after 4 weeks of individualized, consensus-guided traditional Chinese medicine treatment based on syndrome differentiation. Internal consistency (Cronbach α = 0.876) and test‑retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.835) were good. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a single-factor structure (comparative fit index = 0.983; root mean square error of approximation = 0.053). RAPP scores correlated with RQLQ (r = 0.613), AQLQ (r = -0.659), and ACT (r = -0.772; all P < 0.001) and differed across clinical phases and asthma-control levels. Distribution-based indices indicated sensitivity to change (effect size = 0.41; standardized response mean = 0.79). IRT parameters were acceptable overall, although item 7, which assesses the burden of having to take medication, provided less information. No sex-related DIF was detected. Mean completion time was 1.89 minutes. The simplified Chinese RAPP demonstrated acceptable reliability, validity, and feasibility, with preliminary evidence of responsiveness, in adults with CARAS. Its brief format supports routine clinical assessment, follow-up monitoring, and outcome evaluation in research.
keywords: combined allergic rhinitis and asthma syndrome

papers.title: GABAergic inhibition of the nucleus reuniens stabilizes post-learning quiet states and enhances memory consolidation.
papers.abstract: Quiet states provide a permissive context for processes that benefit from reduced engagement with the environment, such as memory consolidation, but the circuit mechanisms that stabilize these states remain unclear. The midline thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) regulates hippocampal-cortical interactions during memory consolidation, but its role in stabilizing post-learning quiet states is unknown. Here, we tested the effects of RE inhibition on quiet-state stability and memory consolidation in freely behaving rats. Following object-place recognition training, rats received RE microinfusions of muscimol or vehicle and we monitored their behavior during the subsequent period. We found that RE inhibition increased the duration of quiet bouts and reduced bout fragmentation. Twenty-four hours later, muscimol-treated rats showed enhanced object-place recognition memory. These findings suggest that RE regulates the stability of quiet states that facilitate memory consolidation and provide a circuit mechanism linking thalamic inhibition, quiet states, and memory function.
papers.journal: Sleep advances : a journal of the Sleep Research Society

papers.title: Drinking Status and Mental Health Symptoms Among First-Year Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Chain Mediation Analysis of Health-Promoting Lifestyle and Sleep Quality.
papers.abstract: The high prevalence of mental health symptoms among college students is a global public concern. However, the research on potential risk factors such as drinking remains insufficient. This study aimed to explore the association between drinking and mental health among college students, and examine the mediating roles of health-promoting lifestyle (HPL) and sleep quality. A single-center cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2272 first-year students from a medical university in Shanghai, China. Drinking status, HPL (measured by HPLP-II), sleep quality (measured by PSQI), and mental health (measured by SCL-90) were assessed. Frequentist structural equation modeling (SEM) and Bayesian SEM were used to examine the mediating associations, adjusting for sociodemographic covariates. Drinking status was significantly correlated with poorer HPL, worse sleep quality, and more psychological symptoms (all p values < 0.001). When HPLP-II score or PSQI score was included as a single mediator respectively, the indirect effects were 0.021 (p < 0.001) and 0.025 (p = 0.010), accounting for 24.1% and 28.7% of the total effect. When the HPLP-II and PSQI formed a chain mediation pathway, the indirect effect value was 0.023 (p < 0.001), accounting for 26.4% of the total effect. Exploratory analyses of the nine symptom dimensions plus the additional factor showed directionally consistent chain mediation associations, and a significant direct association was observed with somatization. HPL and sleep quality may be involved in the association between drinking and mental health symptoms and form a chain mediating association. These findings suggest that HPL and sleep quality may be potential targets for mental health promotion in college students.

papers.title: Does Neurobiological Evidence Support the Diagnostic Distinction Between Hoarding Disorder and OCD? A Critical Narrative Review of Genetic, Neuroimaging, and Neuropsychological Findings.
papers.abstract: Hoarding symptoms were long regarded as one dimension of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but DSM-5 (2013) classified hoarding disorder (HD) as a separate diagnosis. This review asks whether neurobiological evidence, including studies published after the reclassification, adequately supports that decision. This critical narrative review searched PubMed and Web of Science (January 2010 to July 2026, plus foundational studies found by citation tracing) and was structured according to the SANRA criteria. Genetic, neuroimaging, and neuropsychological evidence was judged against four questions: is hoarding a separable trait within OCD; do groups differ biologically on average; is any difference specific to hoarding; and can the evidence classify an individual patient? Twin studies suggest that hoarding-related traits have a heritability of about 26%-48%, and one genome-wide association study reported an SNP-based heritability of 11%. These estimates come from different models and are not directly comparable; they are compatible with a heritable, polygenic trait but do not by themselves show a disorder-specific genetic architecture. A small number of PET, structural MRI, functional MRI, and EEG studies report differences associated with hoarding, including seven direct HD-OCD comparisons, but samples are small, diagnostic criteria vary, and findings have not converged. An exploratory computational study has compared genetic signals for the two phenotypes, but no direct comparison of risk variants exists. Neuropsychological findings were inconsistent: the most recent systematic review found no significant impairment on most cognitive tests in HD. Current neurobiological evidence provides only supplementary, not definitive, support for the diagnostic distinction between HD and OCD. It points to group-level biological heterogeneity, but it does not establish a distinct etiology or individual-level diagnostic utility. Larger studies using standardized DSM-5 criteria and direct HD-OCD comparisons are needed.

papers.title: Foreword: Sleep-disordered Breathing in Heart Failure.
Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding the Long-Term Health Risks of Energy Drink Consumption Among Adults in Iraq: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Energy drink consumption is common among young adults, yet evidence on knowledge, attitudes and practices in Iraq remains limited. This study assessed these domains among adults in Iraq and examined associations of knowledge and risk concern with past-year use and consumption frequency. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Iraq from May to November 2025 using a structured Arabic questionnaire distributed through social media. The sample included 1125 adults. Scale reliability and construct validity were assessed using ordinal alpha coefficients and confirmatory factor analysis. Structural equation models examined associations of knowledge and risk concern with past-year energy drink use and consumption frequency, adjusting for demographic covariates. Past-year consumption was reported by 399/1125 participants (35.5%). Of the 1125 participants, 1002 (89.1%) identified arrhythmias, 977 (86.8%) sleep problems and 794 (70.6%) raised blood pressure as potential risks; 468 (41.6%) reported knowing the ingredients. Support for warning labels, awareness campaigns and age restrictions was 1029/1125 (91.5%), 1023/1125 (90.9%) and 974/1125 (86.6%), respectively. Higher knowledge was associated with greater risk concern, which was associated with a lower likelihood of past-year use and lower consumption frequency among consumers. Energy drink consumption was common in this sample, alongside strong support for regulation and limited ingredient literacy. The findings support clearer product information and targeted public health education.

papers.title: Correction to: 'A registered report testing the effect of sleep on Deese-Roediger-McDermott false memory: greater lure and veridical recall but fewer intrusions after sleep' (2023) by Mak et al.
papers.abstract: [This corrects the article .].

papers.title: In-ear electroencephalography: a systematic review of technology, applications, challenges, and future directions.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to monitor brain activity in both clinical and research settings. However, conventional scalp EEG systems require multiple electrodes, specialised equipment, and trained personnel, which limits their practicality for long-term monitoring in everyday environments. In-ear EEG has emerged as a promising wearable alternative that enables discreet and portable neural monitoring. This systematic review examines the current state of research on in-ear EEG technologies. Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed thematically. The literature highlights rapid progress in device miniaturisation and wearable design, with reported applications including sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive workload assessment, fatigue monitoring, and emotion recognition. Despite these advances, challenges remain related to signal quality, spatial coverage, and motion artefacts. Further research is required to validate in-ear EEG for broader clinical and real-world applications.

papers.title: Orthosomnia: When Perfect Sleep Becomes an Obsession.
papers.abstract: Orthosomnia describes an excessive preoccupation with achieving ideal sleep, often reinforced by consumer sleep technologies and device-generated metrics. As sleep becomes increasingly measured, scored, and optimized, information intended to improve sleep may instead contribute to vigilance, rigidity, and sleep-related stress. This creates a paradox consistent with the attention-intention-effort model of insomnia: sleep depends partly on automaticity and reduced arousal, yet the pursuit of perfect sleep may increase monitoring, effort, and concern about normal night-to-night variation. Consumer sleep technologies can provide useful information, but their outputs may acquire disproportionate authority when interpreted as definitive judgments about sleep quality. Orthosomnia may therefore extend beyond wearable use itself, reflecting a broader pattern of perfectionism, behavioral rigidity, and excessive sleep effort. Clinically, the important question may be whether sleep data remain informative or have begun to govern behavior. For selected patients, management may require less monitoring, greater behavioral flexibility, and renewed emphasis on daytime function and subjective restoration. Perfect sleep may become most elusive when normal variation is treated as failure.

papers.title: Recognizing Pelvic Venous Disease in Chronic Pelvic Pain: A Primary Care Case Report.
papers.abstract: Chronic pelvic pain is a common and challenging condition with a broad differential diagnosis and a substantial impact on quality of life. Pelvic congestion syndrome (PCS) is a clinical manifestation of pelvic venous disease that may involve venous reflux, obstruction, collateralization, and dilation across different pelvic venous territories. Its non-specific clinical presentation and overlap with gynecological, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal disorders may lead to significant diagnostic delay. A 42-year-old woman presented to a general and family medicine consultation with a six-year history of chronic pelvic pain, progressively worsening over the previous six months. She described persistent pressure-like pelvic pain, rated 7/10 in intensity, aggravated by prolonged standing and associated with severe deep dyspareunia, which prevented sexual intercourse, associated with low back pain radiating to the pelvis and both thighs, lower-limb heaviness, and significant sleep disturbance. She denied urinary symptoms or a relationship with the menstrual cycle. During the previous six years, she had undergone repeated medical assessments, with symptoms being attributed to recurrent gynecological infections, probable irritable bowel syndrome, and other non-specific causes. Previous investigations, including colonoscopy and emergency department assessments, had not identified a clear etiology for her symptoms. Physical examination revealed hypogastric tenderness and mild superficial lower-limb varicosities, without vulvar or perineal varices. Pelvic and lumbar computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral dilated periuterine veins measuring up to 13 mm, raising suspicion for a symptomatic pelvic venous disorder. The patient was referred to vascular surgery for further assessment; however, specialist evaluation remained pending at the time of manuscript revision. Pelvic venous disease should be considered in women with persistent pelvic pain, particularly when symptoms worsen with prolonged standing or sexual intercourse and are accompanied by low back pain or lower-limb heaviness. The absence of vulvar varices or previous inconclusive investigations does not exclude a possible pelvic venous etiology. This case illustrates how the non-specific presentation of pelvic venous disease may result in years of fragmented investigation and delayed recognition. Continuity of care in general and family medicine facilitated a longitudinal review of the patient's symptoms and previous investigations, allowing recognition of a pattern suggestive of pelvic venous disease. Greater awareness of pelvic venous disease in primary care may facilitate earlier consideration and appropriate specialist referral in women with otherwise unexplained chronic pelvic pain.

papers.title: Ultrastructure and ligand-gating of the human GluD1 receptor.
papers.abstract: The delta-type ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) GluD1 and GluD2 are ligand-gated ion channels that are fundamental for regulating both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Rising evidence points to the role of GluD1 in the development of neurological diseases. However, the ultrastructure of human GluD1 (hGluD1) and the molecular basis for its ligand-gating remain unclear. Here, we define the ultrastructure of hGluD1 with cryoelectron microscopy and through single channel bilayer recordings, show evidence of its ligand-gating capabilities. While hGluD1 exhibits a nonswapped architecture, it contains conserved iGluR moieties that enable ligand-gating, such as a ligand-binding domain (LBD) tethered to a transmembrane ion channel. Binding of the neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid or D-serine to the LBD enables cation influx through the hGluD1 ion channel in a concentration-dependent manner. Our findings delineate the molecular architecture and function of hGluD1, provide foundations for understanding patient mutations in hGluD1, and will invigorate therapeutic development against hGluD1.

papers.title: Delayed Diagnosis of Bilateral Congenital Choanal Obstruction in a 4-Year-Old Girl: Transnasal Repair with Temporary Stenting and Short-Term Outcome: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Choanal atresia is a rare congenital cause of nasal obstruction. Complete obstruction is termed atresia, whereas partial narrowing is more accurately described as choanal stenosis. We report a 4-year-old girl with lifelong bilateral nasal obstruction, persistent mouth breathing, snoring, poor sleep, easy tiredness, intermittent rhinorrhoea, breastfeeding difficulty during infancy, and recurrent respiratory tract infections. Clinical assessment showed absent right-sided and markedly reduced left-sided nasal airflow. Bedside testing demonstrated no right-sided cotton-wisp movement or misting and minimal movement and misting on the left; a size 8F suction catheter could not be advanced beyond 3.5 cm on the right and met posterior resistance on the left. Preoperative flexible nasal endoscopy was not obtained because financial constraints limited access to the procedure. Computed tomography demonstrated complete right-sided choanal atresia with incomplete left-sided congenital choanal stenosis. The child underwent transnasal repair under general anesthesia using direct visualization with a Killian nasal speculum and headlight, puncture and serial dilatation of the posterior choanal obstruction, and temporary bilateral stenting. The stents were removed after six weeks. During four weeks of follow-up after stent removal, the child had improved nasal breathing and clinically patent bilateral nasal airways. This case highlights delayed recognition of asymmetric bilateral congenital choanal obstruction and the practical diagnostic and operative adaptations required in a resource-limited setting. The outcome should be interpreted as favorable in the short term because objective postoperative endoscopic confirmation and long-term follow-up were not available.

papers.title: Clinical Profile and Reported Functional Impact of Primary Headache Disorders in Children Attending a Tertiary Care Hospital in South India.
papers.abstract: Primary headache disorders are among the most common neurological conditions affecting children and adolescents and are associated with recurrent pain, school-related difficulties, and reduced quality of life. Although migraine and tension-type headache (TTH) are the predominant pediatric headache phenotypes, data from hospital-based settings in South India remain limited. This study aimed to determine the distribution of primary headache phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics, associated symptoms, pain severity, lifestyle-related factors, and reported school-related indicators among children attending a tertiary-care hospital. A hospital-based cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in the Department of Paediatrics, Velammal Medical College Hospital and Research Institute, Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India. A total of 220 children aged 6-15 years with primary headache disorders were enrolled using consecutive sampling. Demographic characteristics, headache profile, associated symptoms, screen exposure, precipitating and relieving factors, school-related indicators, nutritional status, and pain severity were assessed using a structured questionnaire and clinical evaluation. Among the 220 participants, the median age was 14 years, and 125 (56.8%) were female. Tension-type headache was the most common phenotype, occurring in 110 (50.0%) children, followed by migraine in 65 (29.5%), chronic persistent headache in 24 (10.9%), and other primary headache disorders in 21 (9.5%). Most children, 163 (74.1%), experienced headaches on 1-15 days per month, and the mean Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score was 5.28 ± 1.97. Moderate and severe pain were reported by 122 (55.5%) and 52 (23.6%) participants, respectively, while 113 (51.4%) children reported medication use for headache relief. Visual disturbances were reported in 49 (22.3%) children, followed by sensitivity to sound and nausea/vomiting as other commonly reported associated symptoms. Reported scholastic difficulties were observed in 119 (54.1%) children, and school absenteeism was frequently reported. Tension-type headache was the predominant primary headache phenotype in this tertiary-care pediatric cohort. Primary headache disorders were associated with considerable clinical burden, including moderate-to-severe pain, medication use, reported scholastic difficulties, and school absenteeism. Screen exposure was a commonly reported lifestyle characteristic requiring consideration during clinical assessment rather than an established determinant of headache severity. Comprehensive management strategies incorporating accurate symptom recognition, lifestyle counseling, sleep optimization, nutritional assessment, stress management, and evaluation of reported school-related indicators may support appropriate headache care among affected children.

papers.title: Retrospectively Reported Psychological Distress Among Nurses and Nursing Students Following the War Between Iran and Israel: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Crises can significantly affect healthcare professionals' mental health. This study aimed to examine retrospectively reported psychological experiences among Iranian nurses and nursing students in relation to the 12-Day War between Iran and Israel. This cross-sectional study was conducted in Iran in 2025. We recruited 484 nurses and nursing students using a convenience sampling approach. A questionnaire based on the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-28) was used to assess somatic symptoms, anxiety/insomnia, social dysfunction, and severe depression. Higher GHQ-28 scores indicate greater psychological distress and poorer mental health. Over half of participants (n = 272, 56.2%) had GHQ-28 scores above the conventional cutoff of 23; however, this proportion should not be interpreted as the prevalence of psychological distress during the war because the questionnaire was administered retrospectively. The average GHQ score was 27.58 ± 15.04. Longer sleep duration (B = - 0.908, 95% CI [ - 1.682 to -0.135], β = -0.096, p = 0.02) and dormitory residence (B = - 4.876, 95% CI [ - 9.372 to -0.381], β = -0.120, p = 0.03) were associated with lower GHQ-28 scores. Male participants had lower GHQ-28 scores than female participants (B = - 5.556, 95% CI [ - 8.256 to -2.856], β = -0.179, p < 0.001). Participants who had no exposure to explosions (B = - 3.049, 95% CI [ - 5.598 to -0.501], β = -0.102, p = 0.02) had lower GHQ-28 scores. In the additional model, initiation or increase of sedative medication was positively associated with GHQ-28 scores (B = 11.780, 95% CI [7.997 to 15.564], β = 0.280, p < 0.001). The main explanatory model explained 17.4% of the variance in GHQ-28 scores, while the additional model including clinical and help-seeking variables explained 28.6%. Retrospectively reported GHQ-28 scores were associated with demographic, occupational, and conflict-related characteristics among nurses and nursing students. However, given the cross-sectional design, these associations should not be interpreted as causal. Therefore, supporting the mental health of nurses and nursing students may be important for maintaining the quality of care in regions affected by military conflict. Longitudinal studies are suggested to assess changes in GHQ-28 dimensions.

papers.title: Aphasic status epilepticus presenting with prominent psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
papers.abstract: Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is a subtype of nonconvulsive status epilepticus characterized by aphasia as its primary ictal manifestation. Although psychiatric symptoms are uncommon in ASE, they may obscure the diagnosis when present. We report an atypical case, presenting predominantly with agitation and irritability, which was rapidly diagnosed as ASE by electroencephalography (EEG) based on the abrupt symptom onset and neurological history. A 49-year-old right-handed woman with alcohol use disorder was referred to our psychiatric hospital because of agitation, irritability, and disorganized thinking. Approximately 2 months before presentation to our hospital, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days after sustaining a head injury. A left posterior fossa subdural hematoma was diagnosed, and burr-hole evacuation was performed at a general hospital. She continued rehabilitation; however, 6 days before admission to our hospital, she suddenly developed incoherent speech with agitation and irritability, prompting referral to our psychiatric hospital. Neurological examination revealed sensory aphasia. Given the history of brain injury and abrupt symptom onset, EEG was performed and demonstrated left-dominant periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, confirming ASE. Antiseizure treatment resolved the EEG abnormalities and aphasia; however, aphasia, agitation, and irritability recurred with periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. The symptoms improved with intravenous diazepam, and no recurrence was observed for >2 years following optimization of antiseizure medication. ASE may present predominantly with psychiatric symptoms and be misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Recognizing symptom chronology and epileptogenic background is essential for prompting EEG evaluation and early diagnosis.
papers.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

papers.title: Ventricular Pulsed Field Ablation: State-of-the-art Review of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence.
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a paradigm shift in the field of cardiac electrophysiology. The well-demonstrated success with atrial PFA is generating enthusiasm for ventricular applications of PFA, for which the clinical experience is still in its infancy, however. This study is a systematic review and critical appraisal of the published preclinical and clinical evidence on ventricular PFA, involving a total of 111 primary articles (55 preclinical and 56 clinical). An increasing number of PFA platforms and catheters are being used in the ventricle in clinical practice. This appraisal evaluates the impact of ablation parameters in association with lesion depth and volume, and synthesises the available studies of safety and efficacy outcomes for ablation of ventricular tachycardia and premature ventricular complexes with PFA, as reported in case reports and case series from around the world. The cumulative published evidence amounts to a total of 434 patients ablated with PFA for ventricular arrhythmias, with generally favourable acute and long-term results, while the understanding of safety constraints continues to be explored.

papers.title: Etiologic heterogeneity and a common imaging endpoint in reversible splenial lesion syndrome.
papers.abstract: This brief research report describes eight children with RESLES treated at a single tertiary hospital. Etiologies included influenza A infection, respiratory syncytial virus with adenovirus coinfection, clinically suspected enterovirus-related herpangina, autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy (GFAP-A), and one severe infantile encephalopathy with RESLES-like callosal involvement. We aimed to summarize the clinical, laboratory, EEG, and MRI features of these patients and to propose a practical framework in which diverse systemic or CNS insults converge on homeostatic disturbance and cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum (CLOCCs).

papers.title: Neural integration of musical and lyrical emotion: semantic-acoustic congruence in song processing.
papers.abstract: Songs convey emotion through the joint contribution of musical-acoustic structure, lyrical semantics, and vocal-prosodic expression, yet these information sources have often been examined separately in affective neuroscience. This Mini Review synthesizes behavioral, electroencephalographic/event-related potential (EEG/ERP), magnetoencephalographic (MEG), and functional neuroimaging evidence relevant to semantic-acoustic emotional congruence during song processing. Available findings suggest that lyrics and melodies engage partially dissociable but interacting processes during song perception. Early MEG responses around 130-140 ms differentiate lyric and melodic expectancy violations in memorized songs, while N400 modulations provide evidence of context-sensitive meaning-related processing across musical and verbal materials. Later positive components may reflect additional attentional allocation and evaluative processing under conflicting or ambiguous conditions, although their functional interpretations remain task-dependent. Functional neuroimaging studies have implicated superior temporal, middle temporal, and inferior frontal regions in lyric-melody processing, whereas studies of music-evoked emotion more broadly have reported activity in the amygdala, insula, cingulate cortex, hippocampus, and striatal regions. The specific contributions of these regions to music-lyric emotional congruence, however, remain uncertain. Behavioral evidence further suggests that congruence does not uniformly facilitate emotional processing and that incongruence may sometimes increase arousal or alter the relative weighting of musical and lyrical cues. On this basis, the review proposes a provisional dynamic weighted-integration account in which musical-acoustic affect, lyrical meaning, and vocal prosody interact across temporally overlapping processing stages, with their relative contributions varying according to expectations, attention, expertise, and language accessibility. Direct neural evidence specifically manipulating music-lyric emotional congruence remains limited, identifying an important direction for future naturalistic and multimodal research.

papers.title: Case Report: Hyperactive delirium with psychotic symptoms associated with severe hypothyroidism during pembrolizumab therapy. Complete remission after levothyroxine and no recurrence after pembrolizumab rechallenge.
papers.abstract: Thyroid dysfunction is a common adverse event during pembrolizumab therapy, but severe hypothyroidism accompanied by acute neuropsychiatric symptoms is rare. We present the case of a 78-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer who developed agitation, hallucinations, and confusion three months after initiation of Pembrolizumab. Evaluation revealed profound hypothyroidism (TSH 37.9 mU/L, free T3 <0.60 pmol/L and free T4 <0.5 pmol/L) and moderate hyponatremia without acute findings on neuroimaging. Levothyroxine therapy led to complete remission of neuropsychiatric symptoms, and pembrolizumab was safely restarted with close monitoring and no recurrence. This case underscores the importance of assessing thyroid function in acute psychiatric presentations during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and supports cautious rechallenge after stabilization. Severe hypothyroidism was considered a major contributor, although a multifactorial delirium, including the contribution of hyponatremia and the absence of CSF/EEG evaluation, cannot be excluded.

papers.title: Oral breathing and its dental and cognitive implications: a structured narrative review with a pediatric focus.
papers.abstract: Oral breathing is a common condition, particularly in pediatric populations, that has been independently associated with dental abnormalities and cognitive dysfunction. However, these outcomes are often studied separately, limiting a comprehensive understanding of their potential interconnection. This structured narrative review synthesizes current literature to examine both the dental and cognitive consequences of habitual oral breathing and to highlight their possible shared physiological mechanisms, including a hypothesized role of disrupted nasal nitric oxide signaling. A structured PubMed search was conducted in October 2024 using two targeted strategies: one focused on dentofacial health outcomes and another on neurological and cognitive effects. Twenty-three primary studies were included in the evidence synthesis (fourteen dental and nine cognitive), and five reviews and editorials were consulted as contextual background. Across multiple studies, oral breathing is associated with malocclusion, differences in craniofacial morphology, and increased risk of oral disease. Concurrently, research suggests associations with reduced working memory, attention difficulties, altered brain oxygenation patterns, sleep-disordered breathing, and decreased academic performance. By setting these findings side by side, this review proposes a hypothesis-generating framework in which oral breathing is considered a possible marker of broad developmental and physiological risk; no included study examined dental and cognitive outcomes in the same participants. These findings emphasize the importance of early interdisciplinary identification and intervention, particularly within pediatric dental care, and highlight the need for future research exploring causal pathways between respiratory patterns, oral health, and cognitive development. Findings should be interpreted in light of the review's limitations, including reliance on a single database for the primary searches, heterogeneity in the diagnostic criteria for oral breathing, the predominance of observational designs, the absence of a formal risk-of-bias assessment, and reliance on adult experimental studies for several cognitive findings.

papers.title: Association between an improved positioning management strategy and non-incisional low back pain and sleep quality in patients undergoing modified radical mastectomy for breast cancer: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Non-incisional low back pain, particularly low back pain, and sleep disturbance are common yet underrecognized problems during early recovery after breast cancer surgery. This study evaluated whether an improved positioning management strategy was associated with reduced non-incisional low back pain and improved postoperative sleep quality. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult women who underwent modified radical mastectomy or simple mastectomy for breast cancer between January 2024 and December 2025. Patients were grouped according to whether an improved positioning management strategy was implemented during the perioperative period (intervention vs. control). Non-incisional low back pain was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS, 0-10), and sleep quality was assessed using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ: 0-100) at 24, 48, and 72 h postoperatively. Safety outcomes included total drainage volume during the first 3 postoperative days, subcutaneous seroma, and skin-flap ischemia or necrosis. Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts were used for repeated measures, adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), analgesic regimen, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Gamma regression and Firth-penalized logistic regression were applied for safety outcomes. Baseline characteristics were generally comparable between groups, although BMI was slightly higher in the intervention group (P = .04) and was adjusted for in multivariable analyses. Improved positioning management was associated with significantly lower non-incisional low back pain (β = -0.711, P < .001). Pain increased over time in the control group, whereas significant group-by-time interactions indicated greater pain reduction in the intervention group at 48 h (β = -0.358, P = .002) and 72 h (β = -0.737, P < .001). Between-group differences in pain at all time points remained significant after Holm correction. The association remained significant after additional adjustment for incisional pain. Improved positioning management was also associated with higher postoperative sleep quality, with significant group and group-by-time effects at 24-72 h. No significant between-group differences were observed in drainage volume, seroma, or flap ischemia/necrosis. An improved positioning management strategy was associated with reduced early postoperative non-incisional low back pain and better sleep quality after breast cancer surgery, without evidence of increased drainage- or flap-related complications. These findings should be interpreted as observational associations and warrant confirmation in prospective studies.

papers.title: The role of lactate in Alzheimer's disease: from controversies to therapeutic opportunities.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of disrupted brain metabolism, yet the role of specific metabolic intermediates in disease pathogenesis remains incompletely defined. Lactate, long considered a byproduct of glycolysis, is now understood to function as both an energy substrate and signaling molecule that links neuronal activity, glial biology, and network function. In this review, we synthesize clinical, preclinical, and multi-omic evidence to reframe lactate as a dynamic regulator of AD pathophysiology. Emerging data demonstrate that lactate is differentially regulated across disease stages and cellular compartments, with early increases associated with amyloid pathology, reactive glia, and neuronal hyperexcitability. We highlight evidence that disease reactive microglia undergo glycolytic reprogramming and represent a major and spatially enriched source of lactate in the AD brain, challenging the traditional astrocyte-centric view of lactate metabolism. We further discuss how lactate participates in feed-forward mechanisms linking metabolism to inflammation, neuronal excitability, and protein aggregation, but also through epigenetic modifications such as lactylation. Importantly, we propose a context-dependent framework in which lactate exerts both beneficial and maladaptive effects on disease progression. While transient or well-regulated lactate supports synaptic function and cognitive processes, sustained or dysregulated elevations may contribute to neuroinflammation, network dysfunction, sleep loss, and disease progression. Finally, we evaluate the potential of lactate as both a biomarker and therapeutic target. Together, this perspective integrates metabolism, neuroinflammation, and systems-level dysfunction, positioning lactate as a key therapeutic target in AD.

papers.title: Beyond the amyloid-β framework: reconsidering the complementary role of tau-related mechanisms in sleep-cognition research.
A Pilot Crossover Study of the Tsubu-Tsubu Therapy Patch for Refractory Neuropathic Pain.
papers.abstract: Background and objective Nonpharmacological approaches for neuropathic pain are increasingly used, but noninvasive cutaneous stimulation devices remain insufficiently studied. The Tsubu-Tsubu Therapy Patch is an adhesive medical device containing glass beads and is suggested to provide analgesia through noninvasive stimulation based on the gate control theory. We conducted a prospective pilot clinical trial to explore its potential analgesic effect in patients with intractable neuropathic pain. Methods A crossover trial aimed to enroll 26 patients. Patients were randomized to receive the treatment or control patches during Days 1-8 and Days 15-22, with a washout period on Days 9-14. The primary outcome was the between-treatment difference in daily Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores, analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Secondary outcomes included mean VAS differences, PainVision scores, sleep duration, PainDETECT, Pain Disability Assessment Scale (PDAS), Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), and adverse events. Results Nine patients completed the study. Five had postherpetic neuralgia, and four had post-thoracotomy pain. The estimated treatment effect on daily VAS scores was -8.46 mm (95% CI, -11.83 to -5.09; p < 0.001). No significant effects of treatment period or day within the treatment period were observed. No statistically significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes, including mean VAS difference, sleep duration, pain-related measures (PainVision scores, PainDETECT, and PDAS), and AIS. Adverse events such as erythema, itching, and skin indentation occurred in both groups and were not serious. Conclusions This pilot trial found an estimated reduction in daily VAS scores with the Tsubu-Tsubu Therapy Patch compared with the control patch. Given the very small sample size and methodological limitations, these findings should be considered preliminary. Further adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to determine the clinical efficacy of this intervention.

papers.title: Associations between night-time bedroom environmental factors and objective sleep metrics of older adults.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality is associated with adverse outcomes in older adults. Identifying associations between bedroom environmental factors and sleep quality could potentially provide guidance on how to control these factors to improve older adults' sleep quality. Seventeen older adults with normal cognition (4 males and 13 females, mean [SD] age: 76.6 [8.2] years) and 12 with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (11 males and 1 female, mean [SD] age: 77.1 [8.5] years) living in Portland, Oregon were enrolled in the study. Night-time bedroom environmental factors and sleep metrics were objectively collected over a mean (SD) period of 211 (144) nights in participants' personal residences. Mixed-effects models were constructed with six sleep metrics (total sleep time [TST], wake after sleep onset [WASO], sleep efficiency [SE], toss-and-turn count, average heart rate, and average respiratory rate) as outcomes and seven bedroom environmental factors (light, noise, temperature, humidity, particulate matter 2.5 [PM2.5], total volatile organic compounds [TVOC], and carbon dioxide [CO2]) (averaged per night) as predictors including covariates: age, sex, cognitive status, bed-sharing and season. Among all environmental factors, light level had the strongest association with TST (effect size [ES] = -0.051). Relative humidity was most strongly associated with WASO (ES = -0.101) and SE (ES = 0.104). Temperature was most strongly associated with toss-and-turn count (ES = -0.118), average heart rate (ES = 0.052), and average respiratory rate (ES = 0.083), while PM2.5 level was strongly associated with TST (ES = -0.050) and SE (ES = -0.058). All reported associations were statistically significant according to the Bonferroni corrected p-value threshold (p < 0.0083). The results provide insight into which environmental factors should be prioritized when attempting to optimize the sleep environment for older adults. Future work will examine whether environmental effects are different on the sleep of older adults with mild cognitive impairment or dementia versus those with normal cognition.
